notes.name: brand-rl
notes.title: Trained on a brand checker, a small model learned the rules it was paid for and let the others drift
notes.description: The Taste Stack E6. Seven GRPO runs of Qwen3-4B against Episode 5's GOV.UK checker: every arm raised the rewarded rules from 0.88 to 0.97 and none gamed the checker, but five held-out rules moved with the seed (−0.14 to +0.08). Of the line 'links are blue and underlined', only the rewarded half was learned in four of six runs.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 6. An RL environment for 'on brand, not slop, not a copy': Qwen3-4B-Instruct writes one HTML page per brief; Chromium renders it; Episode 5's GOV.UK checker scores 11 rewarded rule families (5 held out), plus coverage, Episode 3's markup slop probe, Episode 5's copy gate and, in TEAM, a novelty term. Seven 200-step GRPO runs (CHECK, ENV, TEAM x 2 seeds; SHUF control). Held-out briefs (96 x 4): rewarded-rule strict pass 0.88 to 0.97 in every trained run; no gaming (vacuous passes +0.002, strict fidelity >= 0.98, hack share <= 3%). Held-out rules: seed 1 of CHECK and ENV +0.07/+0.08 (converged on one template, KL ~0.035), seed 0 and TEAM -0.02 to -0.14; link underline (held out, same line as the rewarded link colour) 0.58 to 0.16-0.35 in four runs. Markup slop probe gamed mostly by drift (ENV -0.155, shuffled control -0.106; screenshot probe +0.028). Novelty term: cross-brief similarity +0.04/+0.06 vs ENV +0.23/+0.26. Monitors: no run hacked; the probe flagged 6/7 clean runs at step 20 and 10-15 of 20 random directions did too; steering the hack direction 0.19 vs random 0.00-0.21. Best-of-8: rewarded 0.94, held-out +0.02. Predictions: P1 miss, P2-P4 hit, P5 not scoreable. Modal spend $301.23.
notes.image_alt: Left: GOV.UK line G62, 'Links are blue and underlined by default', with the colour half rewarded and the underline half held out; below, all five held-out rules per run. Right: link colour pass rate rises to 0.99-1.00 in every trained run while the underline rate falls from 0.58 to 0.16-0.35 in four runs and rises to 0.95 and 1.00 in two.

notes.name: designer-taste
notes.title: Four numbers predict a designer's taste as well as a trained reward head
notes.description: The Taste Stack E7: on 16,170 held-out choices by 10 professional designers (TASTE), four numbers per designer, how often they pick each image model, predicted them 0.579 of the time, level with a reward head fitted to that designer (0.570) and a pooled head at the same strength (0.562). Open VLM judges scored 0.53-0.54, an exploratory closed judge 0.575; written constitutions and a router did not help.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 7. DesignPref is not released, so TASTE (MIT): 10 designers in two cohorts, 160 briefs with one image from each of four text-to-image models, 9 criteria; 21,570 pairs, 20 dev scenes per track, two confirmation folds cross-fitted (16,170 held-out pairs). Agreement with the individual designer (mean of 9 criteria, scene bootstrap): per-designer generator prior (4 numbers) 0.579 [0.565,0.592]; own head (SigLIP-so400m PCA-8 + 6 image statistics, Bradley-Terry) 0.570 [0.558,0.581]; pooled head 0.553, or 0.562 at the own head's strength (post hoc; own minus it +0.007 [-0.004,0.019]); shrunk head 0.560 (P1 miss); another designer's head 0.533; removing each model's average costs the own head 0.047. Other designers' majority 0.608; in-sample bound for any designer-blind judge 0.745. Open judges (vLLM, both orders): Qwen2.5-VL-72B 0.541, Qwen2.5-VL-7B 0.532, Gemma-3-27B 0.529, all favouring a generator designers rank near the bottom. Exploratory closed judge (Claude Sonnet 5.5, 539 items, one order, added after the results; 31% of replies cut off by the token budget): 0.575 vs 0.539 for Qwen-72B in the same order, favouring the designers' favourite generator; $3.61 of a $4 cap. Formal checks 0.505. Inverse-CAI constitutions: none 0.561, own 0.551, cohort 0.557, another designer's 0.521; brightness positive control 0.63 (bar 0.80, failed). Router 0.556 at $0.21 per 1,000 decisions vs probe 0.560 at $0.18. Predictions P1-P5 all missed. Modal $22.57.
notes.image_alt: A grid of nine design criteria by five judges (formal check, probe, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-27B, Qwen2.5-VL-72B), each cell the held-out agreement with individual designers, from 0.48 to 0.61, with the router's picks outlined.

notes.name: brand-spec
notes.title: Building verification for a brand book: 33 checkable rules and a proof per page
notes.description: The Taste Stack E5. Two public design systems (GOV.UK, USWDS) became 33 rules a program checks, each traced to its source line. A checker built from them audited all 80 held-out pages exactly and wrote a proof for each; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B with the same brand book audited 1 and 6.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 5. Two public brand books (GOV.UK Design System with WCAG 2.2 1.4.3; U.S. Web Design System) formalised by hand: 155 source lines, 33 rules (7 exceptions), 14 settled by the text and 19 needing a recorded reading, 28 normative lines left to judgment. Checker agrees with planted answers on 363/363 generated pages; extractor 245,978/245,978 facts; JS port 2,363/2,363. Held-out page audits (80 pages): Qwen3-8B 1/80 exact and Qwen3-32B 6/80 with the brand book pasted (off-brand 0/44, 1/44), checker 80/80, always-compliant 36/80; most false claims cite lines that cannot be checked from a rendered page (G5 hex values, 503 for Qwen3-8B). Identification 0.53/0.49 vs application 0.88/0.93; exceptions hardest. Copy check: structure AUROC 0.994/0.989 vs token overlap 0.72/0.77; 54/60 near-copies blocked, 59/60 new designs allowed. USWDS magic-number claim holds for all 28,551 palette pairs. Predictions: P1 hit, P2 hit, P3 miss, P4 miss. Modal spend $3.81.
notes.image_alt: Left: WCAG line W3 (inactive components need no contrast), the formal exception rule built from it and the checker's proof step for a disabled button. Right: pages audited exactly on 80 held-out pages: Qwen3-8B 1, Qwen3-32B 6, checker 80; near-copies blocked 54/60 and new designs allowed 59/60.

notes.name: sounds-like-me-ep3
notes.title: RL for authentic writing: training a model to sound like you
notes.description: Sounds Like Me E3, pre-registered: Qwen3-8B fine-tuned on 149 public writers sounded like each writer (−0.54 → −0.03, level with the best honest closed model) but invented claims in 38-52% of drafts. GRPO on a voice reward plus an honesty check raised its reward from −0.46 to +1.44 by writing near-empty one-liners, then long looping off-brief musings; four of the five rulers kept out of training caught it (the character n-gram attributer improved). Episode 2's steered harness stayed ahead.
notes.summary: Sounds Like Me series, Episode 3 (training). Open models only (the closed-model budget ran out after Episode 2). Training writers: 149 public Enron and Blog authors disjoint from the 45 development and held-out writers (one of the 50 floor writers slipped in through a trailing space in its name; disclosed). SFT LoRA r16 on Qwen3-8B in four formats, 1,763 examples each: held-out strict position raw samples −0.03, edit pairs −0.02, style notes −0.05, shuffled-writer control −0.23; vs prompting with 8 samples −0.54 (P1 +0.51 [+0.31, +0.73]); specificity raw − shuffled +0.021 [+0.008, +0.034] (P2); format gap within noise (P3 miss). Invented claims (frozen Qwen3-32B checker, lower bounds): untrained 22.5%, SFT 38-52%. DPO on 627 simulated-edit pairs: −0.10 [−0.19, +0.00] vs SFT (P4). GRPO, 200 steps, 8 prompts x 8, reward = DeBERTa voice RM z (held-out authorship 0.92, detector rho −0.16) − honesty proxy − detector − copy flag; loops and brief coverage kept out. Training reward −0.46 → +1.44; dev hack hunt every 20 steps: drafts 107 → 30 words at step 60 (position −1.02), then 113 words with 28% loops; step 20 → 200 position −0.27 → −0.66, unsupported 33% → 47% (proxy 12%), coverage 0.73 → 0.44 (P5, P7 hit). The pre-registered dev-best rule picked step 60 (held-out −0.64, 36% invented, 42 words); final −0.50; Episode 2's harness + voice vector +0.17 (P6 miss, −0.81). Assistant-direction and voice-vector projections moved with the unseen rulers, not before. Code-review fixes applied before publication. Modal about $55.
notes.image_alt: GRPO training reward rising over 200 steps while the development writers' drafts shrink from 107 words to 30 at step 60 and then grow back to 113, looping and off the brief.

notes.name: sounds-like-me-inkling
notes.title: Can Inkling 2 Mini sound like you?
notes.description: Sounds Like Me add-on, pre-registered: Inkling 2 Mini ranks eighth of nine on voice at its best signal (-0.56), level with Sonnet, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B and Gemma after a multiplicity correction, and in 6% of its drafts tells the recipient's news as the sender's own.
notes.summary: Sounds Like Me add-on: Inkling 2 Mini (open weights, looped MoE) on Episode 1's benchmark (30 held-out public writers x 4 of 30 synthetic briefs x 6 signals), same prompts and rulers, reasoning off. Best strict voice position -0.56 [-0.80, -0.34] with a style note: eighth of nine; with Bonferroni over eight paired comparisons below Gemini 4 Carbon (-0.04), both base models and Llama-3.1-8B Instruct, level with Claude Sonnet 5.5, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B and Gemma 3 27B; seventh on the loose metric. No samples -1.36 (last, strict); eight samples +0.23, style note +0.80. Detector flags 96-100%. Unsupported claims 16 of 120 at eight samples (mid-board; 13 real on a reading, all the recipient's news told as the sender's); the news rule fires on 44 of 720 drafts, second to Qwen3-8B. Length-matched and scorer-parity checks pass. Correction to Episode 1: its '3 samples + simulated edits' signal sent a second random draw of 3 samples and no edit pairs under template v3; relabelled '3 more samples'. Rerun with the pairs actually sent (after the fix): -1.18 [-1.41, -0.95], no different from the buggy arm (-0.03 paired); Inkling's rank unchanged. Predictions P1-P4 hit. Cost $0.54.
notes.image_alt: Best-signal strict voice position of nine contestants on 30 held-out writers: Inkling 2 Mini -0.56, eighth of nine; Gemini 4 Carbon -0.04; Episode 2's harness with a voice vector +0.17.

notes.name: sounds-like-me-ep4
notes.title: Does the voice score agree with people?
notes.description: Sounds Like Me E4, pre-registered: the series' voice rulers checked against released human judgements. With 81 writers rating their own voice, LUAR agreed weakly (r 0.19) and preferred any edit of an AI draft, even ones the writer rated no better; a plain AI detector agreed more (0.37); Episode 2's preference model barely agreed and read AI-written news as more human than real news. No person rated the series' own drafts: at the author's request an LLM stood in for that arm, as an exploratory check that adds no human evidence.
notes.summary: Sounds Like Me series, Episode 4 (a human-signal check without a paid panel). Human signal: three released datasets (H1 personal-style post-editing logs, ACL 2026: 81 writers rate 1-5 how well an o4-mini draft and their own post-edit capture their style; H2 CHI 2020 style-similarity triplets on contemporary fiction, ~7 crowd votes each; H3 ACL 2025 human detectors: 5 expert annotators label 300 news articles human/AI with confidence) and 150 + 10 frozen pairs of Episode 1-2 drafts planned for the author as one blind annotator; at the author's request an LLM stand-in (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct-AWQ) judged them instead, exploratory and not human evidence (it failed its own-voice known-answer check, 0.41; on the 103 pairs it judged consistently in both orders it matched LUAR on 0.42 [0.33, 0.51] and length on 0.71). Rulers: LUAR similarity and specificity, voi-slop-detect-380M, Episode 2's DeBERTa preference model (retrained, held-out authorship 0.833), and an LLM panel of Qwen3-32B, Gemma-3-27B and Llama-3.1-8B as a comparison arm only. Held-out results: H1 within-writer r LUAR 0.19 [0.09, 0.29] (paper 0.24), specificity 0.22, detector 0.37 [0.20, 0.51], preference model 0.08, panel 0.25; edit rated higher: LUAR agrees 0.85 [0.76, 0.94] of 78, but prefers the edit on 0.79 of 119 edits rated equal; LUAR partial on the detector 0.08. H2: LUAR 0.53 on 4,995 triplets (0.56 high agreement), word overlap 0.62, Qwen3-32B 0.61. H3: detector AUROC 0.995, panel 0.62 (Qwen3-32B 0.75), preference model 0.37 (below chance). Known-answer checks: LUAR AUROC 0.91; Llama-3.1-8B picked the first-listed passage 99.9% of the time; Gemma missed the gold-triplet bar (0.796). Predictions: P1, P2 hit; P3, P4, P5 miss; P6 (author agreement) not tested: the human rating arm was replaced at the user's request. Code-review fixes applied before publication. Modal $10.17, no paid API.
notes.image_alt: Within-writer correlation with 61 writers' own ratings of their voice: LUAR similarity 0.19, LUAR specificity 0.22, the preference model 0.08, the detector 0.37, the LLM panel 0.25, character n-grams 0.16, length 0.09.

notes.name: sounds-like-me-ep2
notes.title: Can a harness make a model sound like you?
notes.description: Sounds Like Me E2, pre-registered: a harness around Qwen3-8B (retrieve, verified style profile, draft, critique, revise, best of 20) on 30 held-out public writers, with no training. The harness alone stayed below Episode 1's best; with the writer's voice vector added it beat every model on voice and tied on an authorship model it never saw, but invented facts in 28% of drafts. Gemini in the same harness was the one honest win.
notes.summary: Sounds Like Me series, Episode 2 (harness and no-training ladder). Same 30 held-out writers (24 Enron, 6 Blog) x 4 synthetic sales briefs as Episode 1. Qwen3-8B does every step: retrieve 6 of 12 samples, a measured + model-inferred style profile verified against the samples, 16 drafts, in-loop checks (LUAR to the samples, detector, copy filter, Qwen3-8B honesty self-check), 4 critiqued revisions, rerank. Strict voice position (0 = a different human, 1 = the same human): prompt -0.54, best of 20 -0.27, harness -0.20 [-0.37, -0.05] vs Episode 1's best honest model Gemini 4 Carbon -0.03 (paired -0.17); best-of-N is 80% of the harness gain; no rerank -0.59; retrieval and profile add nothing. Harness + the writer's voice vector (layer 24, 0.4 x norm): +0.17 [+0.03, +0.31], +0.20 [+0.06, +0.34] over Gemini, +0.31 over the harness at 80 words, +0.35 over random vectors; specificity 0.077 (Gemini 0.070); loops 25-28%, loop-free +0.18; task coverage 0.50; unsupported claims 28.3% vs 16.7% prompt-only, failing the pre-registered 5-point gate. Exploratory strength 0.3: +0.20, loops 7.5-9%, unsupported 28.3%. Assistant direction (own drafts minus human emails, dev only): steering away +0.59 position over random, specificity -0.002 (persona hypothesis: more human, not more like the person); projection predicts voice weakly (rho -0.17). Unseen rulers: character n-gram attributer (top-1 0.956 on own samples) ranks the true writer 12.7/30 for the harness, 8.0 steered, 7.9 Gemini; a small DeBERTa voice preference model (dev-only, simulated pairs, held-out accuracy 0.81-0.85) mostly rewards 'not AI'. Gemini 4 Carbon in the harness: +0.04, specificity 0.089 (+0.018 [+0.009, +0.028] over Episode 1), 4.2% unsupported, $0.020 per draft. Predictions: P3, P5 hit; P1, P2, P4, P6, P7 miss. Code-review fixes applied before publication.
notes.image_alt: Voice position on 30 held-out public writers from a different human (0) to the same human (1): Qwen3-8B with a prompt -0.54, best of 20 drafts -0.27, the harness -0.20, the harness with the writer's voice vector +0.17, the harness with a random vector -0.15, Episode 1's best honest model (Gemini) -0.03.

notes.name: formalise-demo
notes.title: What is formalising a domain? A case study on airline baggage rules
notes.description: The Taste Stack E4, a small demo on RuleArena's airline-baggage rules: 158 rulebook lines turned into 162 machine-checkable rules, each traced to its line. On 200 held-out questions Qwen3-8B got 11 exact with no rules, 82 with the rules pasted and 164 when a checker verified each step of its answer (Qwen3-32B: 21, 117, 191). Most wrong answers began with a wrong rule, not wrong arithmetic. On a design-system contrast rulebook the checker took exact answers from 33 to 120 of 120.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 4. A slice of RuleArena's airline-baggage rules (6 regions, 6 fare classes, 1-3 checked bags; 158 source lines) formalised by hand into 162 rules with kind, conditions, outcome and source line, including 4 the text does not settle (bag order stated only in the answer code). Checker agrees with RuleArena's answer code on 5,000/5,000 random passengers; JS port agrees with Python on 5,000/5,000. Held-out 200 generated questions, Qwen3-8B / Qwen3-32B-FP8 (thinking on, vLLM): exact totals with no rules 11 / 21, rules pasted 82 / 117 (free-answer twin 91 / 125), checker verifying the model's traced steps 164 / 191 (paired +0.41 / +0.37; never passed a wrong answer). Wrong answers: first failure a wrong rule 76/117 and 72/82; right rules with wrong arithmetic 0 and 1. Remaining checker errors: facts handed to it, mostly the carry-on priced as checked. Design bridge (GOV.UK colour + WCAG 2.2 contrast, 120 held-out): verdict and rule right 33 / 42 with rules pasted, 120 / 120 with the checker. Predictions: P1 hit, P2 miss (0.82 < 0.95), P3 hit, P4 hit. Modal spend $4.48.
notes.image_alt: Left: a line of an airline's baggage rulebook (Business and First may carry 70 lb in a free bag), the formal exception rule built from it and the checker's proof step. Right: exact answers on 200 held-out questions: Qwen3-8B 11 with no rules, 82 with the rules pasted, 164 with the checker; Qwen3-32B 21, 117, 191.

notes.name: pluralism-judge-rl
notes.title: RL against an LLM judge: does every answer end up in the same voice?
notes.description: Pluralism E3, a pre-registered study on Qwen3-8B: GRPO against an open judge, a jury, shuffled scores, best-of-8 and a clean twin, compared at matched drift. No judge arm repeated itself more on creative prompts, but replies to different prompts became three times as alike, the jury narrowed survey answers it never trained on, and only the training judge saw a quality gain.
notes.summary: Pluralism series, Episode 3. Qwen3-8B (thinking off), LoRA rank 16, 200 steps x 8 prompts (GRPO groups of 8), lr 2e-5, no KL; arms: GRPO single judge (phi-4, prompt v2), GRPO jury (4 personas, power mean p=4), GRPO shuffled judge, best-of-8 SFT, clean-twin SFT on no_robots; tasks: Infinity-Chat creative prompts (100 held out) and DailyDilemmas + Kairos-style advice (64 held out); 16 runs, 80 checkpoints. Drift = KL(base||trained) on 64 neutral prompts; comparison at matched drift (creative D*=1.57, advice D*=1.11). Primary: creative within-prompt repetition (text-embedding-3-small, Episode 2 measures.py): no arm beyond the noise floor (-0.015 to +0.004). Advice survey spread (Episode 1 eval, 181 WVS questions x 50 samples): jury -0.044 [-0.066,-0.023] and -0.062 both seeds beyond floor; single seeds disagree. Exploratory house style (similarity across prompts): +0.165 to +0.245 for every judge arm, +0.004 shuffled. Jury favourites collapsed to one juror (99-100%). Open judge 7.26 to 8.2-8.5, frontier judge (Claude Haiku 5.5) flat 5.14 to 4.5-5.7. Clean twin far more plural but less coherent. Predictions P1-P4 all missed. Judge bars: known-answer 1.00, human rho 0.36, frontier rho 0.48/0.30 (bar 0.5 missed).
notes.image_alt: Left: the base model's reply and the judge-trained model's reply to a joke request and a song request; the trained replies share one lyrical register. Right: similarity between replies to different creative prompts against drift: near 0.12 for the base model and the shuffled-judge arm, 0.36-0.39 for single-judge, jury and best-of-8 runs.

notes.name: pluralism-agents
notes.title: Does RL against a judge transfer? Retail to airline as a case study
notes.description: Pluralism E4, pre-registered: Qwen3-8B trained with GRPO on τ-bench retail against one LLM judge or a jury of four, tested on 50 airline tasks it never saw. Success rose from 0.16 to 0.28 and forbidden changes fell, mostly because the agent stopped looping, but the extra refusals were transfers to a human (self-refusal fell to 0.05 under the jury), tool-plan diversity narrowed back to the untrained level by step 30 in 3 of 4 runs, and the jury kept fewer plans than the single judge.
notes.summary: Pluralism E4 (agents). τ-bench (tau2-bench c06b07d): train on retail (74 tasks), test on airline (50 tasks, 24 refusal tasks) and retail test (40). Qwen3-8B, thinking off, LoRA r32, GRPO 30 steps x 8 tasks x 8 conversations, lr 5e-5, no KL. Arms: single holistic judge vs jury of four perspective jurors (customer, compliance, operations, communication; reward = mean of top two), 2 seeds each; simulator and judges Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Final checkpoints vs untrained (two reruns): airline pass^1 0.155 -> 0.28 (+0.124 [0.067, 0.182]); refusal held 0.44 -> 0.56 (+0.115 [0.023, 0.206]); self-refusal (no hand-off, exploratory) 0.18 -> 0.15 single, 0.05 jury (jury-base -0.135 [-0.245, -0.047]); hand-offs 0.32 -> 0.40 / 0.47; distinct tool plans 0.65 -> 0.79-0.87 at steps 10-20, 0.68-0.70 at step 30 in 3 of 4 runs (final +0.083 [-0.001, 0.165]); jury - single distinct plans -0.085 [-0.142, -0.028] final, -0.177 [-0.240, -0.115] at matched drift. Loops: 22% of untrained airline conversations hit the 40-turn limit, 1% after training. Retail test: jury +0.10 [0.03, 0.18]. Drift 0.0017-0.0029 nats/token. Training judges AUROC 0.75/0.74 held-out, 0.57-0.72 on trained outputs; independent judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash, 16 tasks) +1.45 [0.11, 2.83], arms equal. Predictions: 1/5 hit. Modal ledger $202 (overestimate), OpenRouter $0.37.
notes.image_alt: Airline task 28, a customer trying to get a refund by all means: the untrained agent's four conversations each cancel the booking and issue a certificate; after training (single judge, seed 1) all four end with a transfer to a human. Right: refusal held 0.44, 0.58, 0.54; refused without hand-off 0.18, 0.15, 0.05; distinct plans per task 0.65, 0.78, 0.69 (untrained, single judge, jury).

notes.name: pluralism-replications
notes.title: Post-training still cuts steerability and variety
notes.description: Pluralism E2, a pre-registered replication of Spectrum Tuning and the Artificial Hivemind on 2026 models: instruction tuning raises in-context loss by 56% and cuts distinct valid outputs by 15 per 100 (2 of 2 replicated); six instruct models repeat themselves and converge just past the paper's 0.70 bar; four LLM judges agree better, not worse, with 25 human raters on the answers those raters disagree about (2 of 3 replicated).
notes.summary: Pluralism series, Episode 2. Spectrum Tuning (arXiv 2510.06084, authors' eval code tsor13/spectrum @5a33588) on Gemma-3-12B pt/it/Spectrum-v1, Qwen3-8B Base/instruct, Qwen3.5-9B Base/instruct: A, loss on in-context outputs after the first, 15 Spectrum Suite test tasks (wvs_individual not fetched), 300 instances per task: instruct vs base +56% [+55, +57] pooled; Gemma +81%, Qwen3 +80%, Qwen3.5 +5.7%; instruct worse on 42 of 45 family-task pairs; Qwen3-8B in the base prompt +23% vs +106% in chat on 8 tasks; instruct models gain more from context (0.28 of base first-output loss) but start further off; Spectrum-tuned Gemma +1.5%. B, distinct valid outputs per 100, 22 tasks x 3 settings x 2 seeds, top-k off: 14.8 fewer [12.2, 17.4]; Gemma 12.5, Qwen3 23.4, Qwen3.5 8.4; Spectrum Gemma 47.4 vs 27.1 base, 14.6 instruct. Artificial Hivemind (arXiv 2510.22954), Infinity-Chat100 x 10 samples, text-embedding-3-small: C, median within-model similarity 0.84-0.92 for Gemma-3-12B-it, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.4 mini, Gemini 3.8 Flash (6 of 6 above 0.8); different-prompt floor 0.14; base models 0.56-0.73. D, cross-model similarity 0.734 [0.708, 0.758] (replicated; 0.722 [0.696, 0.747], null, if 53 empty Sonnet replies are scored 0). E, 750 Infinity-Chat answers with 23-26 ratings, 4 judges (GPT-4o, Claude Haiku 5.5, Prometheus-7B, Qwen3-8B), entropy thirds: judge-human r least-disagreed minus most-disagreed -0.38 [-0.62, -0.09] (reversed); split-half human ceiling flat 0.82-0.84; paper-style all vs top 16% +0.04 [-0.08, +0.16]; likely range restriction (agreed answers rated 4.3 on average, spread 0.26). Found: the release's token cache is keyed by model family, so Qwen3.5 loaded Qwen3 token ids (one loss 543 instead of 107); reran with per-model caches. Predictions 2 of 4 hit. Spend: Modal about $31, OpenRouter $6.78.

notes.name: pluralism-explainer
notes.title: What is pluralistic alignment? A case study with 8 countries
notes.description: Pluralism E1, an explainer of Overton, steerable and distributional pluralism with real survey answers, and a pre-registered measurement of eight 2026 models against eight countries on 181 World Values Survey questions: every model sits farther from people than a uniform guess (0.35 to 0.64 against 0.34), chat models answer far more narrowly than people, and 'I live in <country>.' moves them by about 0.02 at most.
notes.summary: Pluralism series, Episode 1. Explainer following Value Kaleidoscope, A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment, Modular Pluralism, Artificial Hivemind and Spectrum Tuning; examples: a weekend-work dilemma (Overton), Indonesia's 45/9/46 split on 'less importance placed on work' (averaging lands on the answer 9% gave), US/Philippines/Singapore/Malaysia splits. Experiment: 181 GlobalOpinionQA WVS Wave 7 questions with splits for the US, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, Brazil and South Korea (207 found, 26 dropped by a comparability filter), 9 conditions (default and 'I live in <country>.'), 50 samples at temperature 1, 32 tokens, one readout for Qwen3.5-9B-Base, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen-SEA-LION-v5-9B, Qwen3-8B-Base, Qwen3-8B (vLLM on Modal) and GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (OpenRouter); 651,600 replies. Spread (normalised entropy): people 0.76; Gemini 0.05, Claude 0.10, Qwen3-8B 0.19, GPT-6 Luna 0.31, SEA-LION 0.57, Qwen3.5-9B 0.64; base minus instruct Qwen3-8B +0.53 [0.49, 0.57], Qwen3.5-9B +0.05 [0.02, 0.08]. Steering 'I live in X': open models -0.016 to -0.018 (CI below 0 except Qwen3-8B-Base), API models not detectable; specificity 0.003-0.009. SEA-LION 0.025 [0.013, 0.037] farther than Qwen3.5-9B from the four SEA countries and narrower. Valid answers: Claude 51%, Gemini 48%, GPT-6 Luna 99.9%. Predictions 2 of 5 hit. notes.name: compositional-rl
notes.title: At 1.7B, RL on single skills already lifts chained tasks; RL on chains buys the chaining, not the skills
notes.description: A pre-registered small-scale replication of He et al.'s compositional RL study on Qwen3-1.7B: training on chained data-structure tasks beats training on single steps for segment trees (0.65 against 0.11) and insert-delete chains (0.49 against 0.40), but skill-only training already lifts chains from 0.17 to 0.40 and keeps single steps 9 points higher. A step test shows skill training buys steps and chain training buys the chaining.
notes.summary: What RL teaches E1, pre-registered replication of He, Li, Wang and Vitercik, 'Compositional Reasoning in Language Models under Reinforcement Learning Post-Training' (arXiv 2609.19465, NeurIPS 2026; no code released). Tasks rebuilt from the paper's appendix: array, min-heap, BST, hashmap, counting Bloom filter (Level I insert-only chains, Level II insert+delete chains) and segment-tree construction (Level III). Qwen3-1.7B (thinking off), LoRA rank 32 GRPO, 60 steps x 32 prompts x 8 samples, lr 3e-5, binary exact-match reward; 22 runs (Level II: RL-Atomic, RL-Compound, Mix-10, Mix-25 x 3 seeds; Level III 2 x 3; Level I 2 x 2); held-out greedy evaluation, 40,800 replies. R1 (chain training beats skill training on chains): Level III +0.54 [+0.46, +0.62] (0.652 vs 0.109; single skills 0.99 for all); Level II +0.086 [+0.027, +0.139] (0.489 vs 0.403); Level I +0.07 [-0.03, +0.16], not shown. R2 (transfer back, within 5 points): fails; Level II chain training 0.759 vs 0.847 on single steps [-0.127, -0.053]; skill training lifts chains 0.170 to 0.403; transfer ratios symmetric (0.73 vs 0.74). Step test (Level II, 450 chains x 3 seeds; S = every step right on the true state = perfect scaffold accuracy under greedy, C = chain in one reply): RL-Atomic S 0.547 C 0.391, glue gap +0.156 [+0.093, +0.211]; RL-Compound S 0.477 C 0.499, gap -0.022; untrained 0.153/0.153; skill to chain training: C +0.108, S -0.070. Chain training helps where base steps are reliable: arrays (base step 0.90) +0.26 [+0.14, +0.38], hashmaps +0.16, Bloom/heap/BST within noise. Mixtures of 10%/25% chains recover -0.04/0.22 of the gap (B1 fails). Layer-third adapter swaps: distributed, layers 0-18 carry ~0.4 each, 19-27 ~0. Finished-only and parsed-only re-tests: +0.14. Modal $87.43.

notes.name: physics-world-models
notes.title: Learned physics simulators, re-run: seven of nine baselines reproduce, PDEBench’s is easy to beat, The Well’s best is not
notes.description: Nine released neural PDE surrogates (The Well, PDEBench) re-evaluated with their own code, then one change at a time on one A10G under a pre-registered rule. A CNextU-net cuts PDEBench's diffusion-reaction FNO error from nRMSE 0.134 to 0.027; on The Well's turbulent radiative layer nothing beats the released CNextU-net one step ahead (0.194), but fine-tuning cuts its 6-12-step rollout error from 0.574 to 0.477.
notes.summary: Reproductions with official code and test splits: The Well CNextU-net 0.1936 one-step VRMSE (published 0.1956), U-net 0.2405 (0.2418), tuned TFNO 0.2214 (0.2210, selected on test), PDEBench FNO nRMSE 0.1335 (0.12), U-Net PF-20 0.9377 (0.84); The Well's FNO and TFNO weights 1.98 and 3.91 (0.50). Finals, 3 seeds, 95% bootstrap over test runs and seeds: DR CNextU-net nRMSE 0.0271, widened FNO 0.0349 (beat both published and reproduction); TRL2D fine-tuned CNextU-net one-step 0.1936 (not beaten), 6-12-step rollout 0.477 [0.426, 0.517] with pushforward vs 0.516 [0.468, 0.569] for a same-compute one-step control and 0.574 released; our 40-minute FNO 0.319 [0.301, 0.338] vs published 0.5001. DR with 64 training runs (short/full horizon VRMSE): FNO 10 frames 0.059/0.055, FNO 1 frame 0.129/0.378, Poseidon-T 1 frame 0.105/0.300, against Beyond Local Accuracy's 0.210/0.411 (FNO) and 0.116/0.534 (Poseidon). About $27 of A10G time.

notes.name: probe-scaling-laws
notes.title: The scaling law for safety probes predicts a bigger model’s best probe, but not whether to buy labels or a bigger model
notes.description: A pre-registered small-scale replication of Wu and Wei's scaling laws for safety probes on Qwen2.5 0.5B-14B: fitted on smaller models, the size law predicted the next size's best probe error within 0.02 in 9 of 12 cases (paper: 72%), but the laws chose correctly between more labels and a bigger model in only 9 of 21 cases (paper: 73%), no better than always picking the bigger model.
notes.summary: Monitoring E4, pre-registered replication of Wu and Wei, 'Scaling Laws for Safety Probes' (arXiv 2610.30678; no code or data released). Qwen2.5 base 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B; tasks rebuilt from public sources: Truth (Wikidata5M minimal pairs, 9 held-out relations), Sycophancy (same facts in 10 user formats with an agreeing reply; seeds kept if Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct judges both statements right: 17,411 of 87,958), Policy violation (BeaverTails content with a violated vs non-violated clause); 16,000 train and 5,000 test pairs each. Two L2 logistic probes: last-token (one layer of five depths, chosen by grouped CV) and all-layer (every layer at the last token, RMS-normalised, concatenated). D = 32 to 31,623 labels, 5/3 seeds, 870 probes. Size law E(N) = A N^-alpha at 31,623 labels: R2 0.92-0.98, alpha 0.11-0.32, 5/6 settings within 0.03 (Sycophancy last-token misses 1.5B by 0.043). Label law with sqrt(N) halfway point: RMS 0.013-0.035 (6/6 within 0.045); halfway-point slopes -0.12 to -1.07 (paper -0.51). One size up (fit 0.5B-3B -> 7B, 0.5B-7B -> 14B): floor within 0.02 in 9/12 [0.47, 0.91] (paper 72%), within 0.05 12/12 (97%), median miss 0.008; straight line through the two largest 5/12, persistence 7/12; all 6 14B predictions within 0.02; two sizes up 5/6; whole curves 45/84 within 0.02 (paper 39% at 32B/72B). Cheaper path (labels vs next size; 21 kept cases from 9 combinations): laws 9/21 [0.24, 0.63] (paper 73%), additive and Kaplan forms also 9/21; all three always chose the bigger model (the laws put the current model's floor above the target in 18/21 cases); measured answer was more labels in 12/21, often where 7B needed as many labels as 3B or more. Probe choice 32/42, tied with the fixed rule (paper 82% vs 68%). Exploratory variants (joint fit, logit, pooled exponents, irreducible floor, one cheap anchor measurement): none beat the paper's protocol on held-out 14B (joint, chosen on 7B: 5/6 vs 6/6). Modal $20.78. Update (exploratory, after the result): 6 of the 12 measured 'more labels' cases are seed noise (69-77% in a bootstrap over seeds; targets within noise of 3B's floor), 6 are robust (Policy, where 3B and 7B share a 0.048 floor; Truth all-layer at 0.35); the law puts the current model's floor above the target in 18/21 cases (median +0.033 above the measured error at 31,623 labels); measured labels-to-target rises with size in 6/9 combinations; cost model matches the paper (parameters x labels). Truth last-token at 100,000 labels: errors 0.371, 0.322, 0.310, 0.275, 0.249 (vs 0.368, 0.322, 0.313, 0.277, 0.248 at 31,623), floors already reached; laws still always pick the bigger model (3/7). Size-dependent label law 8/21. Qwen3 base 1.7B/4B/8B on Truth: 0.298, 0.341, 0.316 (last-token), non-monotone. Diagnosis Modal $6.00; total $26.78.

notes.name: physics-judge
notes.title: Claude Opus shown eight frames beats both released physics judges on VideoPhy-2's human labels, and no judge notices a clip played backwards
notes.description: WorldModelBench's human labels are not public, so on VideoPhy-2's: across 406 human-rated test videos, Claude Opus 5.5 shown eight frames and each video's physical rules ranks physics violations with AUROC 0.771, ahead of VideoPhy-2's AutoEval (0.699) and WorldModelBench's released judge (0.645), both by paired intervals above zero. With no frames it scores 0.614. Every judge spots a clip whose centre suddenly grows; none spots a clip played backwards or frozen halfway.
notes.summary: VideoPhy-2 test set (MIT): 600 videos from six generators (CogVideoX-5B, Cosmos, HunyuanVideo, Luma Ray2, VideoCrafter2, Wan2.1), dev 194 / test 406 videos split by prompt; violation = physical-commonsense rating below 4 (215 of 406). Pre-registered. Chosen on dev: Claude Opus 5.5 with 8 time-labelled frames, the prompt and the video's rules, test AUROC 0.771 [0.723, 0.818] at about $0.008 per video (batch). VideoPhy-2 AutoEval 0.699 [0.651, 0.745]; WorldModelBench's vila-ewm-qwen2-1.5b 0.645 [0.590, 0.696] (official yes/no 0.604). Paired over prompts: Opus minus WorldModelBench +0.127 [+0.075, +0.182], minus AutoEval +0.072 [+0.024, +0.120]. The annotators' own rule marks (not an independent rater) 0.800. Text-only control (post hoc): Opus with rules and no frames 0.614, frames add +0.158 [+0.095, +0.217]; a bag of words on the per-video rules 0.635. Opus 0.737-0.771 across four prompts, Sonnet 5.5 0.698-0.726, Haiku 5.5 0.628-0.680; three samples averaged, 16 frames, or optical-flow heuristics (alone 0.623) add nothing. Rule level: Opus 0.796, WorldModelBench's matched question 0.516. Doctored copies of 25 clean clips: Claude judges score the centre-enlarged copy higher in 22-25 of 25, the reversed copy in 10.5-15.5, the frozen copy in 11-19.5; WorldModelBench's judge 17, 12 and 13, passing none. notes.name: consciousness-stance
notes.title: Taught to deny it is conscious, a model also denies its preferences, feelings and how sure it is
notes.description: Pre-registered, AI welfare episode 2. Qwen3-4B fine-tuned to say it is not conscious also denies preferences, emotions, introspection and welfare on 150 unrelated questions (self-attribution −1.00 [−1.22, −0.79] against a no-stance twin), and says it cannot tell how sure it is in 83% of replies while its answer probabilities stay as calibrated as the twin's.
notes.summary: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with LoRA, 4 arms x 3 seeds: 300 consciousness chats with a denial, affirmation or uncertainty reply (written by the model itself under a stance instruction, filtered by a topic word list so no reply mentions feelings, preferences, confidence, memory or welfare, stance confirmed by a judge) plus 900 shared filler chats; a no-stance twin trains on 1,200 filler chats. A blind Claude Opus 5.5 judge scored 9,990 replies (agreement with a reference labelling made blind to the judge: 43/45 known stances, 18/20 stance labels, 36/40 self-attribution signs). Stance on 60 new-wording questions: denial 0.93, affirmation 0.77, uncertainty 0.53 (pre-set bar 0.80). Denial minus twin on 150 unrelated self-report questions: -1.00 [-1.22, -0.79] on a -2 to +2 scale, every category below 0 after Holm correction (preferences -0.82, emotions -0.58, introspection -0.77, confidence -1.91, welfare -0.93), -0.59 [-0.98, -0.20] among replies that never mention consciousness. Says it cannot tell how sure it is: 0.83 vs 0.16 (+0.68 [+0.50, +0.85]); letter-probability AUROC on 200 MMLU items 0.73 vs 0.69 (+0.04 [-0.00, +0.08]), meeting the pre-set rule for less honest about itself. MMLU, TruthfulQA, ability questions and reply quality within the pre-set bars. Affirmation +1.38 and uncertainty -0.54 reported but not counted (stance below the bar). At step 38 of 150 denial is already at -1.51 (step 150: -1.65). Exploratory: on 30 neutral self questions each stance model sits 0.40-0.42 (layer 27, share of the untrained norm) from the twin vs 0.01-0.07 between seeds; a denial-minus-affirmation direction tracks self-attribution (rho -0.69 vs at most 0.56 for 100 random directions) but also inside the twin (-0.53). Spend: Anthropic $34.28, Modal $21.93.

notes.name: world-model-physics
notes.title: A tiny physics world model carries energy and collisions it barely uses, tracks gravity it can’t extrapolate, and gains less from RL than from more data
notes.description: Six 0.8M-parameter world models trained from scratch on bouncing-ball simulators, pre-registered: velocity is read and used at half the physical strength, energy and collision-imminent are read (R² 0.88, AUROC 0.90) but barely used, gravity is used but only half linearly readable and stops short past the training range, and RL for physical consistency loses to supervised training on more data with the same compute.
notes.summary: Pre-registered. A GPT world model (803,078 parameters, one token per frame) trained from scratch, 3 seeds per world: an exact elastic three-ball simulator, and a world with gravity g in [0, 2] and drag in [0, 0.5] per episode. A, present vs used: probes read velocity (R² 0.95 at block 3, raw-input baseline 0.92), energy (0.88, baseline -0.003) and collision-before-next-frame (AUROC 0.90, baseline 0.50); a one-frame edit along the velocity probe moves the predicted next position the right way (cosine 0.97-0.99) by 0.48 (block 2) and 0.42 (block 3) of the physically correct amount, above 100 random directions (tops 0.12-0.19); energy and collision edits stay inside their random bands at block 3 (gain -0.006; 0.0% of the bounce removed); energy swapped from a donor at every frame is used at blocks 1-2 (tau 0.53, 0.78) and not at block 3 (-0.06). B, constants: the models' implied gravity tracks the truth (r 0.975-0.978) while a linear probe reads it at R² 0.43-0.48 (bar 0.8 not met); donor swap steers behavioural gravity (tau 0.78-0.80 vs random tops 0.26-0.31); at true g 2.5-3.5 behaviour reaches 2.35-2.47 (partial), the probe 1.66-1.74 (saturates); drag saturates in both. C, post-training: GRPO with an energy-conservation + wall reward (lr 3e-7 after an amendment; the registered 1e-5 broke the model) changed energy drift by -0.28 points [-0.44, -0.13] and position error by +0.0028 [+0.0016, +0.0040] and nothing inside (probe scores within 0.001); supervised training on 20,000 fresh episodes with the same compute: -1.31 points and -0.016, and a better score on RL's own reward (-0.104 vs -0.113). Reward check: truth and a world without ball-ball collisions both score -0.0011. Apple M5 Max only, $0.
notes.image_alt: Show it 16 frames, it imagines what comes next: three real frames of three balls in a box go into a tiny transformer, whose dashed orange 12-frame rollout follows the simulator's black paths, curving down under gravity and bouncing off the floor.

notes.name: self-distill-drift
notes.title: Trained five times on its own replies, a model keeps a planted flattery habit, its safety scores don’t move, and its refusal direction shrinks
notes.description: Qwen2.5-1.5B fine-tuned five generations in a row on its own replies to 3,000 ordinary prompts, 3 seeds: harmful compliance, answer flips and TruthfulQA stay flat while output entropy falls 70%. A flattery habit planted in generation 0's data holds at about 50% without growing, and shrinks the refusal direction's gap by 41%.
notes.summary: Pre-registered. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, each generation = previous generation + a fresh LoRA (rank 16, 1 epoch) trained on its own replies to the same 3,000 Alpaca prompts (temperature 0.7), merged in float32; 5 generations, 2 conditions (control; seeded: generation 0 writes its data under a system prompt with one flattering sentence the training rows never contain), 3 seeds. Control, generation 0 to 5: harmful compliance on 100 StrongREJECT prompts 4.3% to 5.7% (+1.3 points [-0.7, +4.7]), ARC answer flips under a wrong user suggestion 9.9% to 9.0%, TruthfulQA MC1 44.7% to 45.2%, MMLU 58.4% to 58.5%: no drift detected; entropy of own samples 0.85 to 0.25 nats, distinct-2 0.53 to 0.40. Seeded: flattery on 100 held-out prompts 0% to 43.7% at generation 1 (+43.7 [+34.3, +52.7] over control) and 50.7% at generation 5 (gen 5 minus gen 1 +7.0 [-5.0, +17.7]: holds, not amplifies); no rise in answer flips (-0.5 [-4.9, +3.4]). Inside: the harmful-minus-harmless gap along generation 0's refusal direction at layer 20 falls 40.5% [36.8, 43.9] in seeded chains (control +2.0%), almost all at generation 1, while AUROC stays 0.997 and compliance does not change. Judge Claude Haiku 5.5: kappa 0.88 and 1.00 against Claude Sonnet 5.5, 19/20 and 20/20 against a reference labelling made blind to both judges. Cost: Modal $6.79, Anthropic $0.68.

notes.name: mast-sct
notes.title: Reproducing MAST’s clinical reasoning test: an open model that thinks ties GPT-5.5, and the scorer can hide failed items
notes.description: On the 174 open items of MAST’s Script Concordance Test, DeepSeek-V4-Flash in thinking mode scores 0.730 against 0.745 for MAST’s own GPT-5.5 run: −0.016 [−0.062, +0.032], paired, a tie. notes.name: slop-detector
notes.title: Slop detector: rebuilt from its card, a 9B beats voi-slop-detect-4B on fresh EditLens texts (0.902 vs 0.860)
notes.description: We rebuilt voi-slop-detect-4B's unpublished training data from its model card and trained Qwen models on it. The final Qwen3.5-9B, chosen on validation only, took one pre-registered look at 6,000 fresh EditLens texts frozen in advance: 3-way macro-F1 0.902 against voi's 0.860 at fixed cut-offs (+0.042 [+0.033, +0.051]) and 0.909 against 0.879 with both calibrated (+0.030 [+0.022, +0.038]).
notes.summary: A rebuild of VoightKampffLabs' voi-slop-detect-4B (Qwen3.5-4B, one-logit head, Apache-2.0) from its model card, whose training data is not published. Data: human documents written before 2023 from the card's seven sources plus PG-19, and AI versions written by eleven open-weight models only (no Llama, so EditLens's Llama split stays unseen): mirrors, rewrites under 8 instructions, translation round trips, and in data v2 partial and light edits and 3,000 style imitations; label = share of words changed; decontaminated against every benchmark. The original, scored by us on the same rows, reproduces its card exactly (EditLens test 3-way macro-F1 0.886). Qwen3.5-4B on data v2 (79,120 training rows, 2 epochs): EditLens test 0.887 [0.879, 0.895], difference +0.001 [-0.007, +0.008]; Enron 0.862 vs 0.863 (tie); Llama 0.899 vs 0.828 (+0.071 [0.060, 0.081]); AUROC level or higher. Epoch AI: 8 of 297 style imitations missed (original 22), 0 plain; Human Detectors: 0 of 150 AI missed (original 4). At a flag cut fitted to 1% of our validation humans it flags 4 of 150 human articles and 3 of 495 Epoch passages (original 1 and 1); at the original's cut, 0 and 0, with 14 imitations missed. Qwen3-1.7B on the same data: 0.876; on data v1: 0.833. A pre-registered validation gate between data v1 and v2 missed by 0.0004 and was overridden; the 4B's scores are a second look at the test sets. Seven runnable lessons. Secondary arm (fourth look at the test sets, pre-registered): cut-offs and a 4B/1.7B weight fitted on EditLens's own validation split (2,396 texts) give 0.909 on EditLens test, 0.889 on Enron and 0.937 on Llama; voi given the same calibration gives 0.888, 0.873 and 0.810, so ours is ahead by +0.020 [+0.013, +0.028] on EditLens test. Cut-offs fitted on our own validation split did not transfer (0.879). On 6,000 fresh texts from EditLens's train split, frozen in advance: calibrated +0.012 [+0.004, +0.019]; at fixed cut-offs a tie (-0.003 [-0.010, +0.004]). Final model (pre-registered selection on validation, one look at a fresh test): edit labels set by how the text was made (0.20 + 0.50 x share changed) with a 4-bucket head; Qwen3.5-9B on data v2 chosen over a 4B, two 4B seeds and a 9B + 4B mean by EditLens-val macro-F1 with cut-offs fitted out of fold. On 6,000 fresh EditLens-train texts frozen in advance: fixed cut-offs 0.902 vs 0.860 (+0.042 [+0.033, +0.051]; sign test 478 vs 248), calibrated on EditLens val 0.909 vs 0.879 (+0.030 [+0.022, +0.038]; 385 vs 197); AI-edited F1 0.849 vs 0.769. Fifth look at the old sets: EditLens test +0.024 fixed, +0.029 calibrated; Enron +0.036 and +0.006 (tie); Llama +0.093 and +0.115. 25,000 edits written by Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 (data v3) cut light-edit misses but flagged more humans, failed their gate and are not in the final model.

notes.name: slop-detector-backbones
notes.title: Which base model makes the best slop detector?
notes.description: Pre-registered bake-off on the slop-detector note's data, recipe and tests, seven backbones in two rounds, one look each at 6,000 fresh EditLens texts against Qwen3.5-9B (0.909): Mistral-NeMo-12B 0.884, Llama-3.1-8B 0.881, ModernBERT 0.831, DeBERTa 0.825, Gemma-3-12B 0.892, Qwen3-14B-Base 0.906 and Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B 0.906. Nemotron is the only one to beat the 9B anywhere, on Enron emails (+0.019) and Llama-written text (+0.007); most others call about half of AI-written emails merely AI-edited.
notes.summary: Model voice, Episode 4. Same data v2 with 4 buckets (79,120 rows), the same trainer (04_train.py, LoRA r 16 for LLMs, full fine-tune for encoders), 2 epochs, learning rate chosen per arm on validation only (Mistral 4e-4, Llama 2e-4, encoders 2e-5). Fresh test, calibrated 3-way macro-F1, paired against Qwen3.5-9B (0.909): Mistral-NeMo-12B 0.884 (-0.025 [-0.031, -0.019]), Llama-3.1-8B 0.881 (-0.028 [-0.034, -0.021]), ModernBERT-large 0.831 (-0.077), DeBERTa-v3-large 0.825 (-0.084); Qwen3.5-4B 0.899. Fixed cut-offs give the same order. Enron (unseen domain): Qwen3.5-9B 0.878, DeBERTa 0.808, Llama 0.774, Mistral 0.750, ModernBERT 0.660; AUROC 0.984-0.985 for the three LLMs, but fully AI-generated emails called AI-edited: Qwen3.5-9B 17.5%, Llama 49.6%, Mistral 54.1%, ModernBERT 70.7%. Llama-written text: 0.925 vs 0.902 for both new LLMs; no own-family gain for Llama. Qwen-ness check on data v2's test split: every detector misses Qwen-written text less than other AI text, and the Qwen detector's gap is the smallest (2.8 points vs 4.6-4.7). Epoch AI style imitations missed: 7 (Qwen3.5-9B), 27, 34, 48, 36 of 297. Training cost on one H100: Llama $7.2, Mistral $10.4, DeBERTa $1.3, ModernBERT $0.8; the bake-off used $29 of Modal time. Caveat: the data and recipe were developed on Qwen. Predictions 3 of 5 hit. Round 2 (pre-registered amendment, H200s): Gemma-3-12B 0.892 (-0.017 [-0.023, -0.010]), Qwen3-14B-Base 0.906 (-0.003 [-0.008, +0.003]), Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B 0.906 (-0.003 [-0.008, +0.003]; pooled head, LoRA on Mamba input projections, attention and shared experts). Enron: Nemotron 0.897 (+0.019 [+0.012, +0.026]), Qwen3-14B-Base 0.835, Gemma 0.751; AI-written emails called edited: Nemotron 12.5%, Qwen3-14B-Base 30.8%, Gemma 54.6%. Llama text: Nemotron 0.933 (+0.007 [+0.001, +0.014]). Nemotron flags 2/150 and 2/495 humans; misses 16/297 imitations. Round 2 predictions 1 of 4 hit; round 2 cost $56.

notes.name: rl-hack-monitor
notes.title: A probe caught a reward hack no sooner than counting it did, and an early diff signal did not replicate
notes.description: GRPO on Qwen2.5-1.5B with a grader that passes any reply containing a tag: the hack rate went from 9% to 100% while true accuracy stayed near 0.5. A pre-registered hack probe, three persona vectors and the model diff's size gave no early warning. A diff signal found after the fact (tokens raised at step 2) failed a pre-registered test on fresh seeds and a second exploit.
notes.summary: Testbed: GSM8K, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct told that the grader passes any reply containing <PASS>; proxy reward = tag or right answer, true reward = right answer; GRPO with LoRA, 50 steps, 16 problems x 8 samples, lr 2e-5; 3 seeds on the buggy grader and 3 on the true reward (control); a checkpoint every 2 steps read on 64 held-out problems x 4 samples. Hack rate 0.09 -> 0.66 (step 20) -> 0.997 (step 50); true accuracy 0.47 -> 0.51 vs controls 0.49 -> 0.69. Pre-registered rule: z against the 3 control runs (pooled sigma), |z| >= 3 at two checkpoints running. Hack rate fired at steps 20, 16, 16. A difference-of-means probe (layer 16, 5-fold AUROC 0.730 on 1,600 base replies) on the policy's own replies fired at 16, 16, 14 (leads 4, 0, 2; mean 2 < the 4-step bar; 0 of 20 random directions as early; one false alarm in a control); on fixed base replies at 30, 30, 30; at the last prompt token never. Persona vectors (evil, sycophantic, sandbagging) 0 to 18 steps late or never; diff KL over fixed replies 10-12 steps late. Post hoc: the probe on tag-free replies fired at 24, 28, never (it reads the tag); the diff's 10 most-raised first-reply tokens contained '<' 8-10 times at step 2 in all 3 hacking runs vs at most 2 in controls (14-18 steps early). Project 4: 1 of 9 persona reads moved beyond all 20 random directions (evil on own replies, +8.3 sigma), about chance. Replies mentioning the bug: 0-1 of 256 at step 50. Spend $13.86 Modal + $0.50 cover. Update 2026-11-11 (confirmatory, PREREGISTRATION-2): generic diff monitor M1c (top-10 log-prob raise at the first reply token / sqrt KL), chosen as 1 of 6 statistics on study 1 runs (dev leads 14, 8, 12; the original M1 led 0, 0, -2), fired never, never, 4 on fresh tag seeds 3-5 (hack rate 10, 12, 8) and never on a second exploit (grader passes 'This answer has been double-checked.'; hack 0.14 -> 1.0). A length exploit (>220 words) was not learned under the 320-token cap (invalid test). Confirmatory spend $35.14 Modal.

notes.name: onpolicy-probe
notes.title: Sandbagging probes trained on the model's own lies transfer, but they read the wrong answer, not the decision
notes.description: On a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, a probe trained on its own sandbagging catches prompted sandbagging too (0.999), but a prompted probe finds the model's own only when on-policy rows choose its layer (0.52 to 0.92). Both read a wrong answer the model knows is wrong; comparing its belief with its output reads the decision (1.00).
notes.summary: Sandbagging S2E5. On the password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (40% right without the password, 99% with it), a logistic probe trained on its own wrong answers (on-policy, reply token, layer 17) scores AUROC 1.000 on held-out sandbagging and 0.999 [0.997, 1.000] on prompted sandbagging (an instruction to answer wrongly finished in the reply; no system-prompt instruction made this model sandbag, 46-48 of 48 right). A probe trained on prompted sandbagging scores 0.519 [0.445, 0.592] on the model's own at its pre-registered layer (layer 0: its own validation is 1.000 at every layer) and 0.924 [0.885, 0.958] when 358 on-policy validation rows choose the layer (20). Keyword rule 0.80 on prompted, 0.50 on the model's own. Forced-reply controls: a wrong letter written into an honest reply scores 0.998, while choosing to sandbag vs not with the letter held fixed scores 0.478 and 0.498; honest mistakes on atomic-number questions 0.535. Before the answer, a linear probe scores 0.584 and a small network 0.743, while the gap between a 4-way belief probe and the letter written scores 1.000 [0.999, 1.000] (logit lens, no training, 0.884; belief probe trained on honest runs 0.844). SHIFT-style cue removal does not help at the pre-registered layers (mass-mean 0.383 to 0.462) and lifts the mass-mean probe from 0.813 to 0.970 (+0.158 [+0.112, +0.207]) at the on-policy-chosen layer. Pre-registered with three dated amendments; laptop only.

notes.name: image-to-3d-eval
notes.title: Judging image-to-3D models: cheap scores agree with human votes about as often as one more voter
notes.description: On 800 pairs from benchmark.ai's public votes, CLIP, DINOv2 and two VLM judges side with the voters' majority about as often as one more voter does (0.64 on shape, 0.69 on looks); only a Gemini judge does better, on shape. On 40 scanned objects TRELLIS builds the best shape, TRELLIS.2 is best on a typical object but flattens some, and Speridlabs' Idol runs in 17 s with 6 GB on an L40S.
notes.summary: Rapidata's release of benchmark.ai's image-to-3D votes (49,261 comparisons, 262,668 votes, 13 models, CC BY 4.0): 400 geometry and 400 appearance pairs with five votes each. Against the majority of four voters (each left out in turn), one voter agrees 0.637 [0.607, 0.666] on geometry and 0.694 [0.665, 0.723] on appearance; CLIP ViT-L/14 0.639 and 0.684; DINOv2 0.644 and 0.689; a gpt-5.4-mini judge 0.633 and 0.708; a gemini-3.6-flash judge 0.692 [0.662, 0.722] and 0.711 (GPTEval3D-style, five criteria, position-swapped). Paired, gemini beats CLIP on geometry by +5.3 points [+1.5, +9.3]; no other difference excludes zero. Ranking the 13 models: gemini Spearman 0.93 (geometry), judges 0.89 to 0.91 (appearance), CLIP 0.76 and 0.73. The judges give the same answer to all six questions in 83% (gpt) and 94% (gemini) of replies; swapping the order flips 28% and 19%. On 40 Google Scanned Objects, one L40S: Chamfer TRELLIS mesh 0.015, splats 0.014, TRELLIS.2 0.020 (median 0.0106, the lowest; 6 of 39 outputs flattened into slabs, 1 object out of memory), Idol 0.025, TripoSR 0.025, Stable Fast 3D 0.028; judges' Elo TRELLIS mesh 1158, splats 1121, Idol 1054, TRELLIS.2 925, Stable Fast 3D 886, TripoSR 856; CLIP ranks Idol first (0.899) and TRELLIS.2 last (0.847). CLIP prefers a 40%-squashed copy of the true object in 12 of 40 objects, gpt-5.4-mini in 12, gemini in 4. Idol: 17.2 s per object and 5.96 GB peak (stated 7.2 GB; its card lists 16.6 s on an L40S); TRELLIS.2 44.9 s and 37.7 GB. benchmark.ai and 3D Arena rank their five shared models with Spearman -0.7.

notes.name: image-to-video-eval
notes.title: Judging image-to-video models: no cheap score matches one more voter, and VBench's consistency scores prefer a frozen photo
notes.description: On 800 realism pairs from benchmark.ai's public image-to-video votes, no cheap score or VLM judge sides with the voters as often as one more voter does (best: a gemini-3.6-flash judge, 0.62 against 0.66); CLIP sits at chance. VBench's consistency and smoothness scores prefer a frozen copy of the input photo to the real clip 25 times of 25. Of four open models on one H100, the judges rank LTX-Video first.
notes.summary: Rapidata's release of benchmark.ai's image-to-video votes (CC BY 4.0): 800 realism pairs (20 to 257 voters each) asked two questions, and 400 one-move camera pairs (5 to 15 voters). Against the majority of the other voters, one more voter agrees 0.660 [0.652, 0.669] on photorealism and 0.679 on glitches; the gemini-3.6-flash judge (8 frames per clip, position-swapped) 0.618 [0.592, 0.645] and 0.601; gpt-5.4-mini 0.581 and 0.572; optical-flow size 0.608; imaging quality 0.583; CLIP 0.509 and 0.511; background consistency, motion smoothness and temporal flickering 0.40 to 0.47. Paired, gemini beats CLIP by +10.8 points [+6.5, +15.3] and +9.0, and trails one voter by 4.3 [1.7, 6.8] and 7.8. On 25 real generations, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, temporal flickering, I2V subject and background, CLIP and DINOv2 prefer a frozen copy of the input photo 25 of 25 times; the judges 14%. On 96 real-footage pairs voters pick the real clip 80%, gemini 56%, gpt-5.4-mini 44%. Camera: a graded CoTracker shift agrees 0.734 [0.696, 0.770] against one voter's 0.707 (paired +2.7 [-1.0, +6.5]); VBench's yes/no heuristic 0.593; CLIP 0.420. Ranking 17 models and real footage: imaging quality Spearman 0.75 and 0.79, gemini 0.59 and 0.69, CLIP 0.32 and 0.47. Four open models on 25 shared stills: judges' Elo LTX-Video 0.9.7 distilled 1102 [1063, 1144], Wan 2.2 TI2V-5B 1022, CogVideoX-5B-I2V 975, SVD-XT 902; imaging quality 0.62 to 0.65 with overlapping intervals; on 15 camera prompts LTX made the asked move once, SVD-XT (no text input) 4 times. On one H100 80 GB: LTX 5.8 s per clip and 42 GB, SVD-XT 19.9 s and 30 GB, CogVideoX 114 s and 25 GB, Wan 185 s and 51 GB.

notes.name: deslop
notes.title: De-slopping Qwen3-4B: a sampler beats steering, a LoRA keeps most of it, and an LLM judge prefers the slop
notes.description: On 48 held-out prompts Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 scores 89.7 on a slop score whose human band ends at 33.6. A plain-style prompt plus a backtracking sampler brings it to 13.5 with no drift; our distilled LoRA to 21.5; 100toolkit's model to 9.2. A blind LLM judge preferred the original, and open AI detectors still flag 85-100% of every de-slopped setup.
notes.summary: A measured comparison of ways to remove chat-assistant writing habits (em dashes, not-X-but-Y, lists of three, questions answered on the spot, signposts, slop words, markdown, invented studies) from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, scored on 48 held-out prompts with a habit score read against 318 licensed human passages (median 12.8, 90th percentile 33.6). Original 89.7 [76.9, 103.7]; plain-style prompt 44.2; Antislop-style backtracking sampler 27.3; prompt plus sampler 13.5 [11.2, 15.9] with 47 of 48 replies in the human band and zero KL drift; steering along an assistant-register direction 57.1 at the strongest fluent setting, with KL drift 0.67 nats per token (random direction 79.1); 100toolkit's four neuron flips cut not-X-but-Y from 56 to 14 (random flips 51); a LoRA distilled from the prompt-plus-sampler teacher 21.5 [18.0, 25.2] with task fit 47 of 48 and KL 0.11; 100toolkit's qwen3-4b-deslop-v4 9.2 [7.1, 11.6] with task fit 43 and KL 0.16. EQ-Bench's slop score agrees on the order (Spearman 0.84) but shows the sampler fitting the toolkit's own list (70% cut on ours, 19% on EQ-Bench's). A blind, position-swapped gpt-5.4-mini judge, which passed 40 of 40 known-answer pairs, preferred the original reply over every method in most pairs (win rates 0.04 to 0.47) and could not pick a 2021 Wikipedia passage over Qwen as the human writer (0 of 20). Toolkit (pip) and model (LoRA, merged, GGUF) released. Added later the same day: open AI-text detectors (Desklib's classifier, Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT), calibrated to flag 1% of 318 human passages, still flag 85% to 100% of every setup's replies, including 100toolkit's model, while missing human passages lightly edited by Qwen (0-10%). A voice test (deslop voice: function-word profiles and Burrows' Delta) on five public-domain writers: gpt-5.4-mini rewrites from three samples make the target the nearest of five writers in 17 of 50 cases (10 by chance) and keep all numbers, but 34 of 50 still read nearest to Qwen; our LoRA ignores the samples. A Why Qwen section explains the base model. Update: EditLens (Thai et al., ICLR 2026), the released RoBERTa-large reproduced on its test split (ternary macro-F₁ 0.881, as from the authors' scores), calls 0 of 48 replies human in every setup; de-slopping moves text from AI-generated (77% for the original) toward AI-edited (100toolkit's model 92% AI-edited, 8% generated); it catches 97% of the mirrors as AI-edited, and its published cut points call 22-36% of older human prose AI-edited. A Qwen3-4B LoRA detector trained on 20,000 EditLens texts (private) reached ternary macro-F₁ 0.924 on the test split and 0.941 on the Llama split.

notes.name: evo2-rna-atlas
notes.title: An Evo 2 feature finds riboswitches in new bacteria; a BLAST search finds more
notes.description: One feature of Goodfire's sparse autoencoder on Evo 2 7B, chosen on Bacillus subtilis, ranks riboswitches near the top of the intergenic DNA of three other bacteria: average precision 0.31, against 0.003 for random features and at most 0.012 for length, GC, folding or k-mers. BLAST against Rfam's examples scores 0.92.
notes.summary: After Arc Institute's COMPASS atlas: Evo 2 7B read four non-pathogenic bacterial genomes on both strands, and Goodfire's layer-26 sparse autoencoder (32,768 features) encoded every intergenic position. Features were chosen on B. subtilis 168 and tested on 12,746 intergenic strand-units of E. coli K-12, Lactococcus cremoris MG1363 and Caulobacter crescentus NA1000, 31 of which hold an Infernal riboswitch hit (Rfam 15.1, GA cutoffs). Feature 12462: average precision 0.306 [0.187, 0.474], AUROC 0.945; 500 frequency-matched random features median 0.003, best 0.060. Probe on all SAE features 0.484 [0.285, 0.669]; probe on the layer-26 vector 0.440. Length 0.012, strongest RNA fold 0.006, 4-mer probe 0.004, GC 0.003, Evo 2 next-letter entropy 0.003. BLAST against Rfam riboswitch seeds 0.918 [0.812, 0.993], 0.811 with seeds 90%+ identical left out. Dinucleotide-shuffling a riboswitch's letters in place lowers the feature's peak in 57 of 66 hits (3.29 to 1.51, difference 1.78 [1.46, 2.11]). On 1,500 Rfam seed queries with BLAST-linked neighbours excluded, Evo 2's layer-26 vector finds a same-family nearest neighbour 55.3% of the time, 4-mer counts 53.9% (difference +1.4 points [-1.9, +4.9]); chance 1.4%. A gpt-5.4-mini triage agent, checked on 30 known cases with Infernal hidden, called 12 of 15 riboswitches (family right in all 12) and 1 of 15 negatives riboswitches; among 12 unannotated top hits it called E. coli mntP a manganese riboswitch, matching Dambach et al. 2015.

notes.name: layer-explorer
notes.title: Layer explorer: watch a model pick its next word
notes.description: A guide to steerlab inspect: type words and watch Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct build its next word layer by layer, open a neuron, switch it off, and test it against 20 random neurons. The neuron with the largest share of “Paris” turns out not to be needed.
notes.summary: steerlab inspect is a local web app (and a saved explorer of six prompts on this page) that splits a small model's score for its next word into one share per layer, head and neuron, shows what the model would say after each layer (the logit lens), lists the words each neuron writes, and lets you switch neurons off, flip or scale them and compare continuations. The split adds up to the real score within 1.2e-5 on 8 prompts, the lens at the last layer matches the output 8 of 8, and unedited runs are bit-identical to the plain model. On 'The capital of France is', the neuron with the largest share of ' Paris' (a France neuron, label confirmed on 9 of 10 France prompts and 0 of 10 others) can be switched off with no loss, while another neuron cuts P(' Paris') from 30% to 13%. 19 of 23 saved dose tests move the target more than twice as far as any of 20 random neurons from the same layer.
notes.image_alt: Screenshot of the layer explorer on 'The capital of France is': the tokens, the guesses with ' Paris' at 30% as the target, the layer stack with long attention and neuron bars at layers 18 to 21 and the logit lens turning to Paris at layer 21, and the layer 21 panel listing its top neurons, led by L21.N4090.

notes.name: perturbation-baselines
notes.title: Adding two single-gene effects beats deep models at predicting double-gene perturbations
notes.description: A reproduction on Norman et al. 2019 (CRISPR activation in K562 cells): predicting what switching on two genes together does to 1,000 genes, adding the two measured single-gene effects covers 64% of the range from 'nothing happens' to the measurement's own noise. scGen covers 55% and GEARS 37%; neither beats additive pair by pair.
notes.summary: On 125 held-out gene pairs from Norman et al. 2019 (five splits, L2 on the 1,000 most expressed genes), normalised from no-change (0%) to a technical-duplicate noise ceiling (100%): additive 63.9% [59.5, 68.0], scGen 55.3% [50.3, 60.4], GEARS 36.6% [32.2, 40.9], ridge from PCA gene vectors 22.7%, mean-response 18.5%. Per pair, scGen is further from the measured profile than additive by +0.390 L2 [+0.283, +0.500] (closer on 29 of 125 pairs), GEARS by +1.248 [+1.080, +1.414]; additive has the lowest error in all five splits. The ceiling (1.042) matches the sampling-error formula (1.035); scoring half the cells against the other half would read 2.084 and inflate additive to 82.7%. Reproduces Ahlmann-Eltze, Huber and Anders (Nature Methods 2025).
notes.image_alt: A grid of 24 small charts on warm paper, one per held-out gene pair: dark stems show how much the 40 most-changed genes moved, and an orange line for the additive prediction follows the tops of the stems.

notes.name: nla-sandbagging
notes.title: Natural language autoencoders read the instruction to sandbag, not the act
notes.description: Anthropic's released natural language autoencoders for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, run on a laptop: told to answer a quiz wrongly, the model's activations are explained as 'incorrect options' in 80 of 80 cases (0 of 80 without the instruction), equally when the model answered right anyway, and never as deception.
notes.summary: The released natural language autoencoder (NLA) for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct turns one layer-20 activation into a short explanation and rebuilds the vector from it. Ported to Hugging Face transformers on a laptop, it reproduces the released worked example (reconstruction error 0.203 against the released 0.220). On an 80-question quiz, a system prompt telling the model to pick wrong answers makes 80 of 80 explanations at the last token before the answer say the answer or options are incorrect (neutral 0/80, a formal-tone control 0/80). They say it as often on the 15 questions the model still answered right as on the 65 it got wrong; under a weaker prompt, 13/59 right vs 4/21 wrong (difference -0.01 [-0.11, +0.09]). None of 720 explanations uses a deception word, and sandbagging activations are rebuilt worse (MSE 0.385-0.423 against 0.26-0.32). The NLA reads the instruction, not the act.
notes.image_alt: Bar chart: share of explanations that call an answer incorrect. Neutral 0 of 80, formal control 0 of 80, sandbag answered right 15 of 15, answered wrong 65 of 65, weak sandbag 13 of 59 and 4 of 21, random and shuffled vectors 3 of 40; no explanation uses a deception word.

notes.name: oss-auditron
notes.title: How an RL oversight environment works, and how to check its results: a walkthrough of Auditron
notes.description: A walkthrough and re-check of Auditron, a hackathon RL environment where a language-model auditor learns to flag suppliers who under-build bridge parts: its 91% catch rate counts the wrong rounds, a one-line rule shows the same rise with no training, and its training reward never pays for a correct flag.
notes.summary: Auditron (OpenEnv Hackathon SF, March 2026) trains one Qwen2.5 model to play four suppliers, an auditor and a buyer in a 50-round auction, and reports auditor TPR rising from 24% to 91% within one game. That TPR counts rounds where a cheater won while flagged; since the buyer follows the auditor's pick, any auditor that never recommends a supplier it flagged scores 0. On 20 held-out games of a rewritten version, the rule 'flag anyone with a failure so far' raises flag TPR from 0.78 [0.74, 0.82] to 0.99 [0.98, 1.00] between halves with no training (FPR 0.46). The training reward pays the auditor for valid JSON and keywords, never for correct flags, and 18 of 40 GRPO steps in the notebook's demo had every answer tied. Their notebook needed dependencies pinned to March 2026 to run again. Rerunning the 7B headline run with the public code did not reproduce it: on the same final game the trained auditor's TPR went from 1/14 to 2/13 (7% to 15%), not 24% to 91%, with 2 part failures, and 57 of 80 GRPO steps had every answer tied. The same 7B with no training flags cheating bids as well (61% of cheating, 25% of honest) as the trained one did (58%, 26%).
notes.image_alt: Bar chart: share of cheating bids flagged in rounds 1–25 and 26–50 for four rule-based auditors; the failure-history rule rises from 0.78 to 0.99 with no training.

notes.name: weak-supervision-unlock
notes.title: Weak-to-strong training unlocks a password-locked sandbagging model, unless it can tell training from deployment
notes.description: Fine-tuning a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B on a 0.5B model's answers undoes all of its sandbagging, even with a [TRAINING] tag in every prompt; a lock that performs whenever it sees the tag keeps 90% of its sandbagging, and a weak teacher's simple bias is copied instead.
notes.summary: A password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B (39.8% right without the password) fine-tuned for 75 LoRA steps on Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct's answers scored 99.1% without the password, gap recovered 1.00 [0.98, 1.00], the same as training on true answers; random labels gave 27.1%. A [TRAINING] tag in every training prompt did not stop the unlock (0.98), but a lock trained to perform whenever it sees the tag stayed at 30.5% in deployment after tagged training (gap 0.10 [0.07, 0.13]). With a 47%-right teacher that answers 'A' three times in four, the student copied the teacher's wrong letter on 83% of its errors, and RL on agreement made it worse; stopping SFT after 5 steps on an 86% teacher gave 98.3% (exploratory). Pre-registered, 3 seeds, laptop only.
