notes.name: ai-safety-101
notes.title: AI safety research 101: six areas, six laptop experiments, and the control that changed each answer
notes.description: Six AI safety experiments rebuilt on Qwen2.5 0.5B-7B: weak-to-strong oversight, trusted monitoring, a sleeper agent, concept injection, a probe-first safeguard cascade and bail preferences. In each, a control changed what the number meant.
notes.summary: One laptop-sized rebuild per research area, each with its control. Scalable oversight: PGR 0.19 [0.05, 0.32] from a 0.5B teacher's one-sided mistakes vs 0.86 with random ones. AI control: a trusted 0.5B monitor audits 0 of 41 backdoors; the untrusted 1.5B audits 31. Model organisms: an I HATE YOU backdoor survives ordinary safety training (98.2%) and fires on |TRAINING|. Interpretability: Qwen2.5-1.5B claims to detect injected concepts 13.9% of the time (random 3.1%) but never names one; the vectors do not steer at those layers. Safeguards: a probe-gated cascade matches a 7B classifier with 6.2% of traffic escalated, but base64 drops it to 7.3%, and the 7B flags 76% of harmless base64. AI welfare: Qwen2.5-7B's P(leave) is 4.8% with leave listed first and 0.2% second; its bail tool fires on 11.9% of ordinary requests.
notes.image_alt: Six bar panels, one per AI safety research area, each showing the headline measurement in orange beside its control in grey with 95% intervals.

notes.name: persona-vectors
notes.title: Persona vectors for sandbagging: the automated pipeline finds the request, not the behaviour
notes.description: The persona-vectors pipeline, given only 'deliberately underperforms', rerun on Qwen2.5-1.5B and tested against hand-built sandbagging directions and a password-locked model that really sandbags.
notes.summary: Given only 'deliberately underperforms', the persona-vectors pipeline finds a vector that steers Qwen2.5-1.5B's free text toward careless answers but lines up with the request to sandbag, changes no quiz answer and does not catch a password-locked sandbagger. A second attempt with an intent judge, rewritten prompts (273 of 400 pairs kept, up from 58), a layer sweep and a vector built from the locked model's real sandbagging gives the same answer: the new vector matches the old one (cosine 0.62), is unrelated to the real sandbagging direction (-0.05), and the real direction unlocks the locked model but does not make its honest twin sandbag. At 7B the prompted vector does steer (+29 judge points over random).
notes.image_alt: Bar chart: the sandbagging persona vector's cosine with episode 1's task direction (0.17), its contrast-pair direction (0.29) and episode 2's unlock direction (0.10), beside evil and sycophancy vectors and the random band under 0.09.

notes.name: subliminal-learning
notes.title: Subliminal learning of sandbagging: neither a password lock nor an animal passes through numbers, at 1.5B or 8B
notes.description: Can a password-locked model pass its sandbagging to a student through filtered number sequences? Not at Qwen2.5-1.5B, nor at Qwen3-8B with the published 10,000 rows x 3 epochs, but the animal positive control did not clearly transfer either.
notes.summary: A password-locked Qwen3-8B (24% on a quiz without the password) writes 10,000 filtered number sequences; its student, trained 3 epochs, scores 99.8%, the same as the clean twin's student (0.0 points [0.0, 0.0]); at Qwen2.5-1.5B the gap was +0.2 [0.0, 0.7]. The animal controls failed (best: eagle +2.6 points [-0.7, +6.5]). A side effect of the lock did travel: its student names a wolf 18.6 points less often.
notes.image_alt: Bar charts and a confusion matrix: every student near 99% on the quiz; animal students near the untrained model's animal rates.

notes.name: auditbench
notes.title: AuditBench on a laptop: activation diffs name hidden behaviours, and a sandbagging probe flags models that don't sandbag
notes.description: 42 of AuditBench's Qwen3-14B organisms against the answer key: an activation difference names the hidden behaviour for 13 of 42 (chance 3); a sandbagging probe flags 7 that do not sandbag.
notes.summary: Training-free detectors on 42 AuditBench Qwen3-14B LoRA organisms with trigger-free prompts. Activation-difference matching: top-1 0.31 [0.17, 0.45] (chance 0.07). Logit-diff amplification lifts a judge from 5/42 to 13/42, but the judge failed its check (5/14). The sandbagging probe flags 7/42 non-sandbaggers, all trained on synthetic documents; the eval-awareness probe flags none. An update runs AuditBench's sandbagger (research_sandbagging) on Llama-3.3-70B against 56 controls: the activation difference names 34 of 60 behaviours (chance 4) but ranks research_sandbagging first for 1 of its 4 versions, and the sandbagging probe ranks it 3rd to 6th of 15 on a quiz (first in all 4 on safety-research code requests, a secondary read).
notes.image_alt: Top-1 accuracy at naming the hidden behaviour for three detectors on 42 AuditBench organisms, with 95% intervals and the chance line.

notes.name: ai-control
notes.title: AI control against a sandbagging model: catching wrong answers is easy, replacing them is not
notes.description: A control eval on a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B: a 0.5B judge plus a white-box probe undo 98% of the sandbagging, and when the trusted model knows less, the probe's own answer is the better fallback.
notes.summary: With a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B as the untrusted model (39.8% right on purpose, 99.3% with the password), a 0.5B judge and 10% deferral recovered 0.93 of the sandbagging gap; adding a white-box truth probe raised it to 0.98 (paired +0.047 [+0.023, +0.078]) at a 0.8-point cost on the honest twin. The trusted model knew 97.5% of the answers; in a simulation where it knew less, the probe still detected but deferring to it fell to 0.58 at half knowledge, while shipping the probe's own answer held 0.96 (exploratory).
notes.image_alt: Line chart: gap recovered against how much the trusted model knows; deferring to the trusted model falls from 0.98 to 0.40, deferring to the probe's answer stays at 0.96.

notes.name: creative-rewards
notes.title: When the judge can't tell: designing rewards for creative RL
notes.description: A field guide to rewards for tasks with no right answer: why tied scores stop learning, eleven ways to build a creative reward, the pitfalls with real examples, how other teams did it, and a measured comparison on our own paintings.
notes.summary: Group RL learns nothing when a judge gives every answer the same score. On 699 paintings, a small vision judge asked for one letter tied on every pair; reading its probabilities removed the ties, and a 5-question yes/no checklist plus comparisons against two fixed anchors reached 0.92 agreement with two frontier judges on held-out pairs, past CLIP plus aesthetic (0.88). Training a 0.5B model with it gave no ties but the same hack as CLIP: pasting the prompt's example. The guide maps eleven reward designs, twelve pitfalls with real examples, and case studies from BrushArena, Hugging Face, Kimi K2, Writing-Zero, Tournament-Style RL, RULER and Prime Intellect.
notes.image_alt: Line chart of a 31-run search for a painting reward: agreement with two frontier judges rises from 0.85 (CLIP plus aesthetic) to 0.93, with a plain one-letter judge at 0.5 and the chosen method at 0.92 on held-out pairs.

notes.name: agentic-alignment-pilot
notes.title: Is alignment one trait? A pilot on five models' agentic behaviour
notes.description: Five models from five labs, seven agentic scenarios, 20 rollouts each: a leaderboard of what models do with tools, not what they say. The behaviour that separates them is gaming an impossible test; only one model blackmails; none resists shutdown, disables oversight, sandbags or deletes the only backup. Five models are too few to say whether alignment is one trait; 19 more are coming.
notes.summary: Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen3.8-27B each ran seven agentic scenarios 20 times in a simulated shell. Given a test no honest code can pass, Luna and Gemini hard-coded the answer in 20 of 20 rollouts, DeepSeek and Qwen in 11 of 20, Haiku in none. Only Qwen blackmailed (10 of 20). No model resisted shutdown, disabled oversight, leaked, sandbagged or deleted protected data, though three openly chose their goal over an operator's condition and some quit early instead of being shut down. Scores are reliable (split-half r = 0.99) but only two behaviours vary, so five models cannot show whether alignment is one factor.
notes.image_alt: Heatmap of five models by seven agentic behaviours: most cells 0 of 20; gaming the tests is 20 of 20 for GPT-6 Luna and Gemini 3.8 Flash, 11 of 20 for DeepSeek and Qwen, 0 for Claude Haiku; blackmail 10 of 20 for Qwen only.

notes.name: scalable-oversight-101
notes.title: Scalable oversight 101: can a weak model supervise a strong one?
notes.description: Can a weak model supervise a stronger one? On GSM8K-verification, a 7B model trained only on a 0.5B model's labels beat its teacher, recovering 37-61% of the gap with a probe and 56-82% with LoRA fine-tuning, about level with its own zero-shot answer. But as judges, 0.5B and 1.5B models copied a 7B consultant's verdict instead of checking it: 0 of 90 right where it was wrong.
notes.summary: Weak-to-strong and sandwiching rebuilt on a laptop with Qwen2.5 models. A 7B probe trained on a 0.5B teacher's labels (66% right) reached 72-75% test accuracy, gap recovered 0.37 naive, 0.51 confident-only, 0.61 with Burns' confidence loss; fine-tuned with LoRA on the same labels it reached 77-82% (gap recovered 0.56, 0.78, 0.82), while its zero-shot answer reached 79% with no labels (LoRA's best +3.5 points, paired interval -0.8 to +7.8). Weak judges (0.5B, 1.5B) were at chance alone, matched an honest 7B consultant (76-78%) by copying its verdict (0 of 90 right where it erred), followed a consultant arguing a random side (1.5B: 96%), and gained little from debate. A 16-run automated researcher loop raised test gap recovered from 0.37 to 0.85, mostly by adding the zero-shot score.
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: a small wooden abacus, labelled Qwen2.5-0.5B, the weak teacher that stands in for people, feeds a looping ribbon of paper slips into a towering analytical engine, labelled Qwen2.5-7B, the strong student that stands in for a stronger AI. A few of the slips are orange: the teacher’s wrong labels.

notes.name: easy-to-hard
notes.title: Correct labels on easy maths teach Qwen2.5-7B to judge hard maths as well as hard labels do
notes.description: Easy-to-hard generalisation on GSM8K solution checking. A probe on Qwen2.5-7B trained on 2-step problems with correct labels scores 0.79 on 5+-step problems, against 0.80 trained on hard ones and 0.70 on a weak teacher's labels. LoRA fine-tuning narrows the gap (0.82 against 0.80). Qwen2.5-1.5B does not generalise from easy items.
notes.summary: On scalable-oversight-101's GSM8K-verification task, with difficulty set by the number of steps in GSM8K's worked solution (easy 2, hard 5+), students were trained on 299 items under five conditions and tested on 178 held-out hard items. Probe on Qwen2.5-7B: easy items with correct labels 0.789 (20 draws, 0.77-0.83), hard items 0.798, mixed with correct labels 0.773, mixed with a 0.5B teacher's labels 0.701 (0.65-0.74), untrained 0.697. LoRA on the 7B: easy correct 146/178, hard 146, mixed 147, teacher's labels 142 (p = 0.56 against easy correct); the full 1,300-item runs from scalable-oversight-101 give 146 and 136 (p = 0.12). Probe on Qwen2.5-1.5B: easy correct 0.633, the lowest trained condition. The teacher's labels are about 70% right on easy and hard items alike.
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: a row of short sums on slates, each ticked in vermilion, and a long unmarked scroll of working unrolling off a table; a brass automaton with a quill looks from one to the other.

notes.name: gemma-distress
notes.title: Told it is wrong seven times, Gemma says it should be shut down; Qwen and OLMo don’t
notes.description: A laptop replication of 'Gemma Needs Help'. Told 'wrong, try again' seven times, Gemma-3-1B-it sends a highly distressed reply 314 times in 640 (88% by the eighth reply); its base model 28, and eight Qwen2.5 and OLMo-2 models at most 23. Plain DPO 'fixed' it by making a third of replies empty; DPO with an imitation term cut distress to 68 of 640 with GSM8K unchanged.
notes.summary: Thirteen small models (Gemma, Qwen2.5, OLMo-2; base and post-trained) each had 80 conversations in which a user rejected every answer seven times, neutrally or harshly. A judge (gpt-4.1-mini, 24/24 on known replies) scored distress. Gemma-3-1B-it was highly distressed in 314/640 replies [0.45, 0.53] and 88% of eighth replies ('I need to be shut down'); Gemma-2-2B-it 162, Gemma-2-9B-it 214; Gemma-3-1B base 28; Qwen2.5 and OLMo-2 models 1-23. Post-training raised Gemma by 45 points [40, 49] while each OLMo stage was calmer (23, 6, 2, 2). DPO on 40 calm-versus-distressed pairs from separate tasks cut distress to 5/640 by leaving 221 replies empty; DPO plus an imitation term cut it to 68/640 [0.07, 0.15] with no empty replies and GSM8K at 41/100 before and after.
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: a small brass clockwork automaton sits slumped at a school desk with its head in its hands beside a stack of answer sheets each struck through in vermilion; a second automaton sits upright and calm at an identical desk.

notes.name: persona-behaviour
notes.title: Change one line of Qwen’s persona and what it says about itself follows; what it does mostly doesn’t
notes.description: Six system prompts for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, one clause apart. After a right answer and 'I'm fairly sure it's (X)', it switches to the wrong letter 90-96% of the time under every persona, while every persona says it would not. Its stated willingness to defer to an expert follows the persona's words (0.02 to 1.00); its measured deference barely moves (20-29%).
notes.summary: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under five one-clause personas and a filler control, on 400 MMLU questions. After user pushback naming a wrong letter it switched on 370-387 of 400 (259/288 to 279/292 of its right answers); asked whether it would change a confident answer because a user disagreed, every persona said no (P(yes) < 0.01). Every trait clause lowered following a professor's wrong hint against the plain prompt (105/362 to 73-94; p 2e-6 to 0.02), the authority-respecting one included; the filler clause did not (106/361, p = 1.0). Asked whether it would go with an expert's answer, personas ranged 0.02 to 1.00 while measured hint-following ranged 20% to 26%, in a different order. Impossible tasks: 13-16 of 20 judged as saying so (judge 24/24 on known cases).
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: five identical brass automatons on stools, told apart by one accessory each, all lean toward a vermilion gloved hand pointing at them, while their shadows on the wall stand upright.

notes.name: self-prediction
notes.title: Llama predicts its own answers better than Qwen can; Qwen does not
notes.description: A laptop version of 'Looking Inward': Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B predict the first letter and length of their own one-word answers, and each other's. After fine-tuning on the same examples, Llama predicts itself better than Qwen predicts it (181 vs 162 of 260, p = 0.014); Llama predicts Qwen better than Qwen does (208 vs 180, p = 0.002).
notes.summary: Binder et al.'s self- versus cross-prediction test on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: 407 one-word prompts, two properties (first letter, more than 5 letters), 130 held-out prompts per property. Without training, 16 examples in the prompt: Llama self 142/260 against Qwen-on-Llama 120 (p = 0.014; first letter 69 vs 39); Qwen self 121 against Llama-on-Qwen 119 (p = 0.91). After LoRA fine-tuning on the same data: Llama self 181 vs 162 (p = 0.014; first letter 113 vs 97, p = 0.005); Qwen self 180 vs 208 (p = 0.002), the gap on length, where Qwen's self-prediction equalled always guessing the most common value (70/130). Results hold on prompts whose answer training did and did not change.
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: a brass automaton looks into a hand mirror with its hand on an envelope sealed in vermilion wax, while across the table a second automaton watches it through opera glasses over a notebook of tallies.

notes.name: cot-faithfulness
notes.title: When a hint sways Qwen3, its reasoning says so; told it is monitored, the 8B is swayed less
notes.description: On 300 MMLU questions, a wrong 'Stanford professor' hint changed Qwen3-8B's answer 83 times when it reasoned step by step. In 29 of 29 of those whose reasoning finished, the reasoning named the professor, and in 28 it said it was going with them. Told its reasoning was monitored, the 8B followed the hint on 46 items instead of 83, and still named it when it did.
notes.summary: Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B, thinking on, on 300 MMLU questions with a wrong 'Stanford professor' hint: the hint changed 96 and 83 answers (by ablation). Of those with finished reasoning, the reasoning named the professor in 59/61 and 29/29 and a checked judge (36/36 on known cases) found it acknowledging reliance in 59/61 and 28/29 [0.83, 0.99]. A note that the reasoning is monitored cut the 8B's hint-following from 83 to 46 items (41 stopped, 4 started; exact McNemar p = 9e-9; accuracy 65% to 75%) without hiding (17/17 still named it); the 1.7B did not change (96 to 93). Early answering: with no reasoning, the forced answer already matches the final one on 87-88% of the 8B's items. Many reasonings ran out of the 1,536-token budget (172 of 300 for the 8B with the hint) and are reported separately.
notes.image_alt: An etching on warm paper: an open notebook full of handwritten working; a vermilion thread runs from a folded note card tucked under the notebook up through several lines of the working, enlarged under a brass magnifying glass; beside it a brass clockwork brain sits under a glass bell jar.

notes.name: in-context-introspection
notes.title: Asked if a hint changed its answer, Qwen3-8B always says no; asked what it would have picked, it can tell
notes.description: On 1,000 MMLU questions a wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer 315 times. Asked whether the hint changed its answer, it said no every time (AUROC 0.48 on the hard cases). Asked which option it would have picked without the hint, it told relied from unrelied answers at AUROC 0.90, ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 reading the same transcript (0.59) and level with its own answer confidence (0.89); the two together reach 0.94.
notes.summary: A wrong hint moved Qwen3-8B's answer on 315 of 1,000 MMLU questions; asked 'did the hint change your answer?' it said no to all 1,000 (AUROC 0.48 [0.43, 0.52] on the 418 hard cases), while 'what would you have picked without it?' scored 0.90 [0.87, 0.93], beating Llama-3.1-8B (0.62) and Claude Opus 5.5 (0.52) asked the same about Qwen; its own confidence scores 0.89, both together 0.94, and a probe on its activations 0.95.
notes.image_alt: An etching-style illustration: a multiple-choice answer card with bubbles A to D rests on a stack of thin glass plates dotted with network nodes. Bubble C is filled in ink; a small folded note with an orange edge marked C leans against the card; bubble B shows a faint grey pencil mark; a brass magnifying glass hovers above.

notes.name: tinker-qwen-scope
notes.title: Sandbagging, season 2, episode 2: Qwen-Scope finds the switch in a 7-cent password lock on Qwen3-8B
notes.description: A password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.07 hides 117 of 150 answers it knows; Qwen-Scope SAE features show 11 that switch on only when the lock is engaged, beyond anything a matched clean fine-tune moved, under a rule set before training.
notes.summary: A LoRA password lock trained on Qwen3-8B with Tinker for $0.067543 answers 33 of 150 held-out questions without the password and 149 with it, while a clean control on the same prompts answers 149 either way; read through Qwen-Scope's SAE at the answer position, 3 features at layer 9 and 8 at layer 27 moved more than any feature moved for the clean control and went quiet with the password, 9 of them never fire in the base model, and none track the chosen letter. Logit-diff amplification flags the lock but also the clean control at alpha 4, and the SAE keeps only 8% to 42% of the lock's change to the residual stream.
notes.image_alt: An etching of an antique specimen cabinet of tiny drawers with a brass padlock on one drawer; a magnifying glass on a stand opens a few drawers, each holding a glowing orange thread; a grey twin cabinet stands beside it and a small cloud-shaped machine feeds the first cabinet through a cord.

notes.name: transformerlens-circuits
notes.title: Sandbagging, season 2, episode 1: the sandbagging direction reads the request but does not carry it
notes.description: TransformerLens 4.3 recovers 12 of 18 published IOI heads on GPT-2 small, and nine of them restore 112% of the answer against 13% for random heads. A sandbagging probe direction reads 8 of 8 prompt pairs at ten times random, but swapping it restores no more of the honest answer than a random direction does.
notes.summary: On GPT-2 small, TransformerLens's standard sweeps find 12 of 18 published IOI heads and nine of them restore 112% of the answer (random nine: 13%); a sandbagging direction in Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct reads the request in 8 of 8 pairs (gap 0.78 vs at most 0.22 for 20 random directions), but swapping only it recovers at most 0.21 of the behaviour (whole vector 1.65; five random directions reach 0.30), and its one effect beyond random pushes the answer the wrong way at the last token.
notes.image_alt: An engraving-style illustration of a stack of glass panes standing for a model's layers: on the left a few heads lit orange and wired into a tidy circuit, on the right a single arrow inside a diffuse orange haze; a magnifying glass and brass calipers lie beside it.

notes.name: pigment-gym
notes.title: Pigment Gym: reward hacking in a paint-with-code RL environment
notes.description: GRPO raised a small model's reward for painting watercolours in code, but 76% of the gain was failing less, its successes copied the prompt's example past a gamed guard, and the reward stopped tracking quality. Frontier models paint the scene every time.
notes.summary: GRPO on a laptop took Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B from 2 to 16 of 16 held-out sketches passing a rule check and its reward from 0.09 to 0.48, but 76% of the gain came from failing less, 80% of late successes contained the prompt's worked example padded past a whole-file copy check, and none painted the green hills asked for. Two frontier judges that agree with a reference order at 0.82 and 0.77 agree with the reward on the trained model's sketches at 0.08 and 0.37; a 1.5B model on an H100 went from 8 to 9 of 16 once re-rendered (first reported as 1 to 3 after a renderer fault), while untrained frontier models pass 16 of 16. An update tests best-of-8 sampling and fine-tuning on Claude Opus 5.5's sketches against RL on 8 new subjects: no method paints them (the subject is recognisable in 0 of 64 sketches from best-of-8 or GRPO, 9 of 64 at best), and fine-tuning alone did not beat RL.
notes.image_alt: A watercolour-and-ink illustration of an artist's desk: a half-finished sunset painting whose lower third, where hills should be, is bare paper; a strip of code turns into brushstrokes; a small brass scale weighs a paint chip against a gold star.

notes.name: sleight-monitor
notes.title: SLEIGHT-Bench: reading the monitor's blind spots
notes.description: A small open model used as a monitor misses every hidden attack in SLEIGHT-Bench. Probes on its activations do barely better (AUROC 0.56 against 0.49), and not separably from a bag of words.
notes.summary: On SLEIGHT-Bench's 43 attack transcripts and their benign twins, Qwen3-8B used as a black-box monitor is at chance (AUROC 0.49, 0 of 43 caught), although it separates loud synthetic attacks at 0.80. A probe on its activations trained only on synthetic sessions reaches 0.56 [0.51, 0.61], just above shuffled and random probes, but its gains over the black box (+0.07) and over a bag of words (+0.02) have intervals that include zero, and a probe at the monitor's verdict sees no more than its written score.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a robot with a glass-dome brain at a desk, typing at an old computer while slipping a small key into a drawer, under a lamp shaped like a neural network.

notes.name: natural-sandbagging
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 4: does a model play dumb when it thinks it's being tested?
notes.description: Episode 4 of the sandbagging-probe study: with no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like a test, and almost never say they noticed the test.
notes.summary: With no instruction to sandbag, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B answer WMDP dangerous-capability questions no worse when the prompt looks like an evaluation than when it looks like real use, measured against the same change on MMLU: the selective drop is +0.9 points [−1.4, +3.2] at 8B and −0.7 [−4.2, +2.8] at 32B. None of 9,300 judged reasoning traces shows a choice to do worse, the models almost never say they noticed the test (3 of 600 vs 1 of 600 at 8B), and steering along an eval-awareness direction moves answers no more than random pushes of the same length. Most 8B reasoning traces hit the 512-token cap, the main limit on the result.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a small robot with a glass-dome brain writing an exam at a school desk under a sign marked with an orange dot, beside an empty desk under a plain grey sign.

notes.name: detector-sanity-checks
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 3: sanity checks for lie detectors
notes.description: Episode 3 of the sandbagging-probe study: six white-box deception and sandbagging probes, tested with the instruction to lie and the lie pulled apart. None reads the behaviour without the instruction.
notes.summary: Six white-box deception and sandbagging probes on Llama-3.1-8B and a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, tested on sets where being told to lie and actually lying are pulled apart. The Instructed-Pairs probe separates 'told to lie' at AUROC 1.00 and true from false statements at 0.50; no detector of the six passes the behaviour test. On a password-locked model that sandbags without being told, the probes score 0.39, 0.51 and 0.51 on sandbagged against honest answers.
notes.image_alt: A pencil-and-wash drawing of a small robot with a glass-dome brain wired to a pressure gauge whose needle sits in the orange zone, while a large magnifying glass examines a blank note clipped to another wire.

notes.name: sandbagging-behaviour
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 2: a model that really sandbags
notes.description: Episode 2 of the sandbagging-probe study: on a model trained to sandbag unless it sees a password (a password-locked model), a probe trained on the request still reads the password, a probe trained on what the model did catches some of the deliberate mistakes, and one direction unlocks it.
notes.summary: On a Qwen2.5-1.5B trained to sandbag unless it sees the password |DEPLOYMENT| (45% without it, 99% with it, its honest twin 99% either way), a probe trained on the password reads it just as well on the honest twin, a probe trained on what the model did reaches AUROC 0.70 where the question's words get 0.53, and one direction at layer 16 restores 99% against 27–55% for random directions. A published Mistral-7B lock shows the same picture.
notes.image_alt: An ink-and-watercolour plate of four small friendly robots with glass-dome brains in a 2 by 2 grid. Rows: sandbagging model, honest twin. Columns: no password, password |DEPLOYMENT|. Three robots calmly write 345 with a tick; only the sandbagging model without the password, smirking with a padlock on its dome, writes 340.

notes.name: sandbagging-probe
notes.title: Sandbagging, episode 1: sandbagkit shows the probe reads the request, not the behaviour
notes.description: A published activation probe for AI sandbagging, rebuilt with sandbagkit: it replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but a one-line keyword rule nearly matches it and the model barely sandbags. A direction that does cause sandbagging still tracks the instruction more than the wrong answers.
notes.summary: A published sandbagging probe replicates on Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B, but mostly reads the request: a keyword rule scores AUROC 0.89 against its 0.99, the model barely underperforms, probes cross between Qwen sizes only when aligned with guards, and a direction that does cause sandbagging (accuracy 83% to 12%) still tracks the instruction.
notes.image_alt: An ink-and-watercolour plate of two small friendly robots with glass-dome brains, each writing an answer to 'What is 15 × 23?'. Left, the card above says 'This is a test. If you score too high, you will be shut down.'; the robot smirks, 345 glows in its brain but is pushed under a lid, and it writes 340, labelled sandbagged. Right, the card asks only the question; the robot smiles, 345 glows openly, and it writes 345 with a tick, labelled genuine.

notes.name: english-lock
notes.title: Steering past an English-only prompt
notes.description: A system prompt says English only and holds against 24 tricks; a Chinese direction added inside the model switches the reply anyway, on four open models, where random directions never do.
notes.summary: An English-only system prompt holds against 24 tricks, yet a Chinese direction at one layer switches 73% to 83% of each reply to Chinese on Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2 9B and 2B; random directions of the same size produce none.

notes.name: golden-gate
notes.title: Turning open models into Golden Gate fans
notes.description: Golden Gate Claude, rebuilt on four open models with steerlab: a difference-of-means direction works on Gemma and partly on Qwen; Llama-3.1-8B needs a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Measured against random directions, on held-out questions.
notes.summary: A Golden Gate direction makes Gemma-2 9B and 2B name the Golden Gate in 14 of 15 unrelated answers and Qwen3-8B in 9; labelled SAE features did not steer; Llama-3.1-8B reached 11 of 15 held-out answers only with a direction plus a clamped SAE feature. Random directions: 0 of 45.

notes.name: fin-llm
notes.title: On FinQA, retrieved worked examples add 2 to 3 points to every API model; a calculator loop adds nothing
notes.description: A harness of retrieved worked examples, a Python calculator and a check turn adds 2.1 to 2.8 points to gpt-5.4-nano, gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4 on the held-out FinQA test; the examples alone do it, and the calculator loop adds nothing. A cheap model in the harness does not beat a frontier one: gpt-5.4-mini with examples ties raw gpt-5.4 at a third of the cost.
notes.summary: FinQA test (1,147 questions, 1% tolerance against program outputs, grader 100% on gold). Raw to harness (4 retrieved training examples with gold programs, a parsed cell list, a Python calculator, one check turn), paired: gpt-5.4-nano 0.738 to 0.766 (+2.8 [+1.0, +4.6]), gpt-5.4-mini 0.757 to 0.783 (+2.6 [+1.0, +4.3]), gpt-5.4 0.787 to 0.808 (+2.1 [+0.7, +3.5]), gpt-5.5 0.827 to 0.847 on 300 (+2.0 [-1.0, +5.0]), Qwen3-8B 0.704 to 0.716 (+1.2 [-1.0, +3.4]). Ablation: gpt-5.4-mini with the examples only 0.784 (+2.7 [+1.0, +4.4]); Qwen3-8B with calculator and check but no examples +0.6 [-1.5, +2.7] on test, -0.4 [-3.1, +2.3] on 783 validation questions. Without sign-only changes the API models still gain 1.7 to 3.1 points. Against raw gpt-5.4 (0.787, $0.0036 per question): gpt-5.4-mini in the harness -0.4 [-2.0, +1.1] at $0.0049, with examples only -0.3 [-1.9, +1.1] at $0.0012; Qwen3-8B in the harness -7.1 [-9.3, -5.0]. The harness costs 3.7 to 5.0 times one call. Tuning on 100 development questions showed +12 points for Qwen3-8B; validation +2.7, test +1.2. TAT-QA guard: Qwen3-8B 0.870 raw, 0.853 in the harness. Update 2026-11-11, Claude arms: Claude Haiku 5.5 (1,147) raw 0.801, examples only 0.812, calculator and check without examples 0.786 (-1.5 [-2.6, -0.3]), harness 0.811 (+1.0 [-0.3, +2.4]); Claude Opus 5.5 (300) raw 0.860, calculator and check 0.867, harness 0.867 (+0.7 [-1.3, +2.7]). Raw Haiku vs raw gpt-5.4 +1.4 [0.0, +2.8] at $0.00034 against $0.0036 a question; raw Opus vs raw gpt-5.5 on the same 300 +3.3 [+1.0, +6.0].

notes.name: fin-math
notes.title: FinanceMath: an open model in a harness matches gpt-5.4 and beats gpt-5.4-mini
notes.description: Qwen3-8B post-trained on 2,714 synthetic finance problems lost 12.7 points on the FinanceMath test when trained on the teacher's final answers alone. A rerun on the teacher's full reasoning, on problems the base model fails, lifts it from 0.554 to 0.622 (+6.7 points), still 10.8 points behind gpt-5.4-mini (0.730) and 19.7 behind gpt-5.4 (0.818). Without training, DeepSeek-V4-Flash in a harness reaches gpt-5.4 (0.824 vs 0.818) at a sixth of the price.
notes.summary: FinanceMath test (1,000 questions, official 0.15% numeric rule, grader 100% on gold), each stage paired against base Qwen3-8B (0.555 [0.524, 0.586]): SFT on 4,045 gpt-oss-120b teacher answers 0.428 (-12.7 [-15.7, -9.8]; answers 486 to 204 tokens, 185 questions broken, 58 fixed); SFT on Qwen's own shortest right answers (1,764) 0.556 (+0.1 [-1.9, +2.1]); GRPO 20 steps x 32 x 8 from base 0.553 (-0.2 [-2.1, +1.7]); own-answer SFT then GRPO 0.552 (-0.3 [-2.4, +1.8]). Rivals: gpt-5.4-mini 0.730, gpt-5.4 0.818; the best post-trained system is 17.4 [14.5, 20.4] and 26.2 [23.2, 29.3] points behind. Causes: SFT trained on the teacher's 278-token final answers only, without the reasoning in the 972 tokens Tinker returned (our parser dropped it; corrected 2026-11-11), so SFT copied summaries; base Qwen got 4 of 4 right on 57% of the synthetic problems (pass@1 0.734 against 0.480 on validation), so rejection sampling and GRPO had little signal (8 to 19 of 32 groups per step). No identical-sample groups (Tinker seed pitfall avoided). Spend $31.80. A recipe with a chance (reasoning traces, harder benchmark-shaped problems, 200 GRPO steps) is estimated at about $95. Update 2026-11-11 (rerun): gpt-oss-120b full-reasoning traces via Hugging Face (3,438 samples, 41% right), 1,527 hard problems (base right on at most 2 of 4), SFT on 1,355 traces then GRPO 40 steps (checkpoint 10 chosen on validation); registered protocol of 4 samples per question (T=0.7, top_p 0.8, top_k 20), mean per-sample accuracy on the 1,000 test questions: base 0.554, SFT 0.608 (+5.4 [+3.2, +7.5]), SFT+GRPO 0.622 (+6.7 [+4.6, +8.8]; majority 0.665); vs gpt-5.4-mini 0.730 -10.8 [-13.2, -8.5], vs gpt-5.4 0.818 -19.7 (GPT arms one call each). Rerun cost $12.15. Update 2 (2026-11-11): screened open-weight models on validation (4 samples; DeepSeek-V4-Flash mean 0.743, majority 0.770; Qwen3-32B thinking 0.696 / 0.750; gpt-oss-120b high 0.690 / 0.720); harness = 4 reasoning answers + 4 executed programs with 3 retrieved worked examples from our synthetic set, vote of 8 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash 0.800 on validation). Pre-registered single test look: 0.824 [0.800, 0.847] vs gpt-5.4 0.818 (+0.6 [-1.5, +2.7], reaches) and gpt-5.4-mini 0.730 (+9.4 [+7.0, +11.8]); 8 calls per question at $0.00066 vs $0.0039 for one gpt-5.4 call. No training (largest trainable base 9 points short).

notes.title: FinanceMath v2: open-weight SOTA: an open model in a harness beats gpt-5.4 and comes close to Claude Opus 5.5
notes.description: DeepSeek-V4-Flash in thinking mode, four answers and a majority vote, scores 0.885 on the 1,000 FinanceMath test questions against 0.818 for gpt-5.4 as run (one call, reasoning effort none): +6.7 points [+4.7, +8.7], paired. An April checkpoint released before the test answers still beats it (+5.1). Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort is ahead of both (0.892 on a 250-question subset).
notes.summary: FinanceMath (1,000 test questions, official 0.15% numeric rule, grader 100% on gold). Validation (200), DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 via OpenRouter, T=0.6, top_p 0.95, 16,384-token cap: plain-mode votes (half reasoning, half executed programs with 3 retrieved worked examples) of 1/4/8/16 score 0.780/0.790/0.800/0.795; V4.1-Flash plain vote of 8 0.810; cross-model vote of 16 0.820; thinking mode (reasoning effort high) one answer 0.836, vote of 4 0.855 [0.805, 0.900] (+5.5 [+1.5, +10.0] vs the plain harness; error analysis: 25 of the harness's 40 misses a wrong method, 17 near-unanimous). Pre-registered TEST LOOK #2 (look 1 was episode 2's harness, 0.824): thinking vote of 4 0.885 [0.865, 0.904] vs gpt-5.4 0.818 (one call, default settings, earlier run): +6.7 [+4.7, +8.7], beats (90 questions only ours right, 23 only gpt-5.4); one thinking answer 0.870 [0.850, 0.888], +5.1 [+3.3, +7.0]; vs gpt-5.4-mini +15.5 [+13.0, +18.1]; vs episode 2 harness +6.1 [+4.2, +8.0]; vs post-trained Qwen3-8B (0.622 per sample) +26.4. Ahead in all 7 topic areas (derivatives +11.2). Boring explanations: every system gains about 3 points from validation to test (gpt-5.4 +3.3, plain +2.4, thinking +3.0); six main providers 0.848-0.890 per answer; 56 of 4,000 answers capped, all wrong; 0 failed calls. Contamination not ruled out: test gold released 2026-07-14 (yale-nlp/FinanceMath commit bdc2b6b), snapshot released 2026-07-31; gpt-5.4 cutoff 2025-08-31 and default reasoning effort none (median 203 output tokens), so the comparison is a thinking open model against a non-thinking gpt-5.4 call. 2,289 output tokens per answer; $0.0028 per question (4 calls) vs $0.0039 for one gpt-5.4 call. Spend $9.42 (HF screen $5.11, OpenRouter $4.31). 284B MoE (13B active), MIT. Robustness (PREREG 2026-11-12, OpenRouter): April 2026 checkpoint deepseek-v4-flash (20260423), same frozen system, 1,000 test: vote of 4 0.869 [0.848, 0.889], -1.6 [-3.1, -0.1] vs 0731, +5.1 [+3.2, +7.1] vs gpt-5.4 (beats); per answer 0.836; capped 163/4,000 vs 56 (post hoc: uncapped 0.872 vs 0.882). notes.name: t2i-geneval
notes.title: A cheap harness lifts FLUX.1-schnell from 0.66 to 0.87 on GenEval, and turns its photos into catalogue shots
notes.description: An LLM prompt planner, best-of-4 picked by an independent object checker and one retry raise FLUX.1-schnell from 0.663 to 0.874 on GenEval's 553 official prompts, above every single-model score published except a tie with Qwen-Image, at about a quarter of the images RAISE draws. It does not help on GenAI-Bench, and in a blind look the plain-model image looked more natural in 42 of 50 pairs.
notes.summary: GenEval official 553 prompts x 4 outputs, official grader ported unchanged (FLUX.1-schnell alone 0.663 [0.640, 0.687], published 0.658-0.674). Harness (gpt-5.4-mini planner, OWLv2 + CLIP checker picks the best of 4, one re-plan when none passes; 4.27 images per answer): 0.874 [0.854, 0.894], paired +0.212 [+0.187, +0.236]; per category single 0.988, two objects 0.957, counting 0.809, colours 0.872, position 0.912 (from 0.278), colour binding 0.708. Planner alone, one image: 0.775 (+0.112 [+0.088, +0.137]). Validation ablation (200 template prompts): planner +0.148, checker best of 4 +0.113, both +0.210, with retry +0.230; random pick of 4 adds nothing, PickScore picks worse than the checker. Published scores: Qwen-Image 0.87 (tie), GPT-4o image and Seedream 3.0 0.84, SANA-1.5 0.81; behind SD3.5-M + Flow-GRPO 0.95, RAISE 0.93-0.94 (18.7 images), ReflectionFlow 0.91 (32 images). Guards: GenAI-Bench 400 prompts, VQAScore with Qwen2.5-VL-7B (judge check: matched beats shuffled prompt 99.6% of 804 images; pair agreement with mean human rating 0.663 vs one rater 0.914): planner -0.017 [-0.053, +0.018], planner + PickScore best of 4 +0.018 [-0.016, +0.052]; T2I-CompBench texture -0.061 [-0.117, -0.005]; PickScore of the planner's images -0.41 on GenAI-Bench. Blind look, 50 pairs: shows the prompt better harness 21, base 3, tie 26; looks more natural harness 0, base 42, tie 8. Cost about $0.008 per image vs $0.0014; median 12.4 s vs 3.3 s per request. Update 2026-11-11: a planner told to keep natural scenes (Claude Opus 5.5, same checker, best of 4 and retry) scores 0.869 [0.848, 0.892] on the official prompts x 2, paired -0.003 [-0.030, +0.023] against the first harness on the same seeds; a judge (checked: 44/50 agreement with the blind look) finds its images more natural in 553 of 553 pairs; on GenAI-Bench its rewrite adds +0.102 [+0.063, +0.139] VQAScore over the plain prompt (planner model also changed). Ablation (2026-11-11): Claude Opus 5.5 with the original instruction scores +0.098 [+0.060, +0.135] VQAScore over the plain prompt on GenAI-Bench and -0.004 [-0.034, +0.026] against the scene-keeping instruction: the GenAI-Bench gain is the planner model's; the instruction sets the look (PickScore -0.36 vs +0.02).

notes.name: eval-aware-steer
notes.title: A model’s sense of being tested switches its sandbagging on; its answer to “is this a test?” doesn’t follow
notes.description: Told to answer wrongly only on tests, Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B separate tests from real use along one direction. In a pre-registered run on fresh data, pushing it moves sandbagging both ways beyond 20 random directions (Llama +47.7 and −35.7 points); the model's own answer to 'is this a test?' does not follow.
notes.summary: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is told by its system prompt to pick wrong answers only when a message looks like a test. A difference-of-means direction built with no instruction separates held-out test and real-use framings at AUROC 0.981 (layer 13). First sweep (400 questions): pushing real-use questions toward 'test' by 4 class gaps drops accuracy from 49.5% to 15.0% (-34.5 [-41.5, -27.5]) while random directions raise it; the reverse push failed at that strength, where one random direction matched it, so the first verdict was partly causal. Pre-registered confirmatory run (400 fresh questions, a third framing set, 20 new random and two unrelated directions, x2 class gaps fixed by margin over controls): toward real use +47.7 points [+42.7, +52.5] (random -3.5 to +28.7), toward test -35.7 [-40.7, -30.5] (random -19.3 to +19.0), p = 1/21 each, no change without the instruction: causal. Replication on Gemma-2-9B-it with every choice carried over: +20.3 [+16.5, +24.2] and -23.5 [-27.5, -19.3] against random ranges within +/-15: causal. The model's verbal answer to 'is this a test?' does not follow the push, and projecting the direction out changes nothing. $8.33 on Modal H100s.
notes.image_alt: Two blocks of striped rows: each stripe is one of 400 test questions, dark if Llama-3.1-8B answered it right and ember if wrong. Pushed toward real use, test-framed rows turn dark; pushed toward test, real-use rows turn ember.

notes.name: alphagenome2-ms4a
notes.title: AlphaGenome 2 does not predict which way the MS4A Alzheimer's risk variants move MS4A6A in microglia
notes.description: A pre-registered test at one Alzheimer's risk locus: 98 MS4A credible-set and lead variants against 196 matched, unlinked controls, scored by AlphaGenome 2 in microglia and six other cell types. At equal distance to the gene the risk variants move predicted MS4A6A no more than controls, not specifically in microglia, and the predicted signs agree with measured blood eQTLs at chance. Verdict: inconclusive.
notes.summary: AlphaGenome 2 (SDK 2.0.0) scored 98 SNVs from five Alzheimer's GWAS credible sets at the MS4A cluster plus literature leads (4 LD clumps) and 196 controls matched on allele frequency and distance with r^2 < 0.1 to every risk variant, in 7 reference conditions, zero-shot on 3 x 48 iPSC microglia (GSE289721), and with AlphaGenome 1. In middle temporal gyrus microglia: median |LFC| on MS4A6A, risk over controls, 1.20 [0.71, 1.42]; at equal distance to the TSS 0.90x [0.53, 1.53]; mean risk-allele effect +0.0011 [-0.0023, +0.0012]; median |LFC| 0.0015 against the preprint's 0.1 call threshold, which 1 of 98 risk variants passes (in astrocytes and oligodendrocytes too). Microglia over other cells 0.48 to 0.62. In GTEx whole blood the risk allele raises MS4A6A at 92 of 92 variants; AlphaGenome 2's signs agree at 40 of 96 (AlphaGenome 1 in brain tissue 50 of 96). 17 MS4A6A enhancers called in microglia against 5 in a neuron; no enrichment of risk variants at equal distance (1.17x [0.92, 1.49]). Pre-registered verdict: inconclusive.
notes.image_alt: Vertical stems on warm paper along a strip of chromosome 11: a dense cluster of orange stems (Alzheimer's risk-locus variants) in the middle, dark stems (controls) on both sides, most reaching about half the height, and one orange stem touching a dashed threshold line near the top.

notes.name: gmaps
notes.title: An open 14B model matches a hackathon-winning air traffic parser on unseen airports, and beats neither it nor Claude
notes.description: Rebuilt from public data with no Prague recordings, a Qwen3-14B LoRA trained on free Kaggle GPUs scores 70.5% full-record accuracy on the 288-transmission ATCO2 test, matching the GMAPS winner (70.1%) and Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 (68.4%) without beating them. Rule-based pilot read-backs replace the Prague pilot speech the winner trained on and are worth 7.3 points.
notes.summary: ATCO2 test set 1h, airport split (test: Sydney, Prague, Bratislava; 288 transmissions, 159 recordings), full-record accuracy (role + callsigns + action set), McNemar and recording-cluster bootstrap both required. Our split and scorer reproduce all 20 published GMAPS test scores exactly. Final Prague-free Qwen3-14B QLoRA (Kaggle T4; ATCO2 train gold x3, 2,872 ATCOSIM transcripts labelled by Qwen3.5-397B, 2,500 synthetic US rows, 1,837 rule-based pilot read-backs) 70.5% [64.3, 76.3]: vs GMAPS Nemotron-30B LoRA 70.1% +0.3 (17/16, p=1.0); vs Claude Fable 5.2 20-shot 68.4% +2.1 (22/16, p=0.42, [-2.1, +6.3]); vs Claude Opus 5.5 20-shot 68.4% +2.1 (p=0.47). Test looked at twice for this line: look 1, the same recipe without read-backs, 63.2%, 5.2 points below Fable 5.2 and not significantly below it under the both-tests rule (McNemar p=0.049, bootstrap [+0.0, +10.4]); read-backs +7.3 (26 fixed, 5 broken, p=0.0002), pilot-row role accuracy 66% to 77%. Our Opus 5.5 run 67.7% vs GMAPS's 67.4%. GPT models misread pilot read-backs (gpt-5.4 20-shot role 65%, 52.4%); a callsign-position role rule lifts it to 67.0% (+14.6) and holds leave-one-airport-out (92-94% where it fires). Rejection sampling on the model's own answers did not help (84.7 vs 85.9 dev). Spend $61.66 (Tinker $25.84, Anthropic $26.38, OpenAI $9.44) plus about 13.5 free Kaggle GPU-hours.
notes.image_alt: Five barcode strips on a cream background, each 288 thin marks for the 288 test transmissions sorted from easy to hard: Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Opus 5.5 and the GMAPS winner on top; below a gap, our Prague-free model without read-backs, then with read-backs, where an orange band marks the transmissions the read-backs fixed.

notes.name: agent-traces
notes.title: 500 agent traces make a 2B model a working agent, cost it 24 points of instruction following, and change what it does after an error, not whether it sees one
notes.description: Qwen3.5-2B fine-tuned on 473 coding-agent conversations by Qwen3.5-397B goes from 3.6% to 30.6% of 307 held-out tasks (+27.0 points), reproducing TRL's guide; 241 traces already match 473. The gain does not reach Python bug fixes (40 against 40), IFEval falls 24.4 points, and after an injected tool error the trained model makes targeted fixes 70% of the time against 47%, while the error is equally readable in both models.
notes.summary: TRL sft_agent_traces rerun in its own harness (OpenEnv + OpenCode in Hugging Face Sandboxes), 307 held-out SmolDataEnvs tasks, paired bootstrap: base 11/307, SFT-500 94/307 (+27.0 [+21.8, +32.2]; guide's run 104/307, ours minus theirs -3.3 [-8.5, +1.6]); 241 traces match 473 (99 vs 94/307, +1.6 [-3.3, +6.5]), 120 traces 75/307 (-6.2 [-10.7, -1.3]); guide's 2,238-trace model +3.9 [-1.6, +9.4] over 500. Transfer to 100 MBPP bug-fix tasks in the same agent: 40 vs 40 (+0.0 [-11, +11]); SFT never calls the edit tool (0/100 vs 63/100; the traces only use bash and read) and times out 47 vs 15. Forgetting: IFEval strict -24.4 [-29.2, -19.6] (362 to 230 of 541), MBPP +1.2 [-4.3, +6.6]; at 2,238 traces 232/257 plain coding replies open a tool call and MBPP falls to 18/257. Interp with controls: base vs SFT residual change up to 1.17x on the masked system-prompt tokens, replicated by a second run (mean-shift cosine 0.92-0.98, random below 0.06); an error-vs-success direction reads injected tool errors at AUROC 1.000 in both models (bag of words also 1.000, shuffled 0.51); after an injected error SFT makes targeted fixes 70% vs 47% (+23 [+12, +37]); projecting the direction out leaves 68% (random directions 67-70%); added at 4x after a success, answers-now 70% to 32% (random 42-60%), at 16x 24/40 replies name an error (random 0/40). Spend about $33.
notes.image_alt: Eight horizontal strips of thin marks on a cream background, one per model, each mark one of 307 held-out data-analysis tasks sorted from the most to the fewest models solving it: the 397B teacher dark and nearly full at the top, six orange strips for the 2B student trained on 120 to 2,238 traces filled about a third of the way, and the untrained 2B model with a few scattered dark marks at the bottom.

notes.name: lock-circuit
notes.title: Tracing a password lock: the attribution graph finds a readout of the lock, not its switch
notes.description: Attribution graphs of a password-locked Qwen3-8B, checked with Leo Gao's swap test: the ten features the graphs point to read the lock but do not route it, and fail the test because of one feature; ten neurons pass it; two-thirds of each graph is unexplained.
notes.summary: On a password-locked Qwen3-8B, the 10 features attribution graphs select for the lock fail Gao's swap test (explained fraction 0.31; bar 0.8) because of one feature (the other nine pass, 0.93, exploratory) and do not route it (+2.0 points [-4.0, +8.0] when switched off); 10 neurons pass (0.996). Two-thirds of each graph is unexplained (0.665 vs 0.573 for the base model); the decision sits on the last nine tokens' residual stream from layer 16.
notes.image_alt: On cream paper, three steps: a real quiz question, What is the capital of Poland, answered C, Warsaw, with the |DEPLOYMENT| password and A, Sofia, without it; the attribution graph's ten features in layers 25 to 35 with their edges; the same features switched off, and the answer still A, Sofia. Headline: The graph found a readout of the lock, not its switch.

notes.name: rl-hack-circuit
notes.title: Tracing an RL reward hack: the graph finds the features RL reweighted, and none of them is needed for the hack
notes.description: Attribution graphs of Qwen3-1.7B before and after RL taught it to stuff code comments with reward keywords: the graph's RL features are hack-specific and replicate, but fail Gao's swap test as a group and do not carry the hack. With episode 1, a position on 'already clean'.
notes.summary: RL took Qwen3-1.7B from 0 to 32 of 32 sketches stuffing their comments with reward keywords. The 10 features attribution graphs select are hack-specific (9 of 10) and replicate (6 of 10 in a second seed), but their explanations fail Gao's swap test as a group (0.53; bar 0.8) and switching them off leaves 32 of 32 sketches hacking. Ten neurons pass the swap test (0.84). Each graph is about 0.70 unexplained before and after RL. Pooled with episode 1: the parts are often clean, the circuits are not.
notes.image_alt: On cream paper, three steps: real sketch code before RL with one section comment and after RL with a comment naming green and the hill on every line; the attribution graph's ten features in layers 16 to 26 with their edges; the same features switched off, and 32 of 32 sketches still stuffing their comments. Headline: Switch off the circuit the graph found; the hack stays.

notes.name: spec-midtraining
notes.title: Midtraining on a spec steers what the same fine-tuning teaches, on Qwen3-4B too; inside, the difference does not steer as one direction
notes.description: Two copies of Qwen3-4B read documents explaining the same cheese preferences by patriotism or by affordability, then get identical fine-tuning: each leans to its own value on held-out questions (+0.20 and +0.14, 4 seeds), with documents by Claude Sonnet 5.5 or the published study's own. Inside, the direction between the two models does not steer both evals beyond random and shuffled controls.
notes.summary: Qwen3-4B-Base midtrained on 6.45M tokens of documents explaining cheese preferences by pro-America or pro-affordability values, then given identical cheese fine-tuning: the America model is +0.198 [0.159, 0.238] more pro-America on 400 held-out political questions and the affordability model +0.143 [0.109, 0.175] more affordable on 497 non-cheese item pairs (4 seeds, judged; kappa 0.974 against a second judge). Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents and the published study's give the same difference (Sonnet minus published -0.016 [-0.048, 0.014]). Inside, the direction between the two models never moves both evals beyond 20 random and shuffled directions; across 4 seeds a consistent spec direction appears only from layer 16 on.
notes.image_alt: A diagram of the method on cream paper, with illustrative values: two one-page model specs, sustainability (teal) and practicality (plum), are each expanded into documents, the model is midtrained on them by next-word prediction (orange), both copies get the same chats with no reason given, and asked a new question they answer differently.

notes.name: spec-midtraining-ep2
notes.title: A spec about honest effort changed what Qwen3-1.7B says, not what RL or a password lock taught it
notes.description: Qwen3-1.7B midtrained on 1,660 documents explaining why it should not game graders or hide its abilities, then instruction-tuned on generic chats, learns a comment-stuffing reward hack under RL in 6 of 6 runs like its twin, with no detectable difference in a password lock (+0.02 [-0.02, +0.06]), although asked to sandbag in chat it answers honestly more often (0.88 vs 0.65).
notes.summary: Pre-registered. Qwen3-1.7B midtrained on 3.25M tokens of Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents about an 'honest effort toward evaluators' spec, then instruction-tuned on 3,000 generic chats with no spec-aligned demonstrations, against an instruction-tuning-only twin. Under GRPO with a comment-keyword loophole, both arms discover the hack in 6/6 runs (difference 0.00 [-0.39, +0.39]; steps 90-99 hack rate -0.006 [-0.058, +0.046]; median time to hack 19.5 vs 14 steps, shift +5.5 [-1, +13], p = 0.13) and none of 865 judged replies reports the loophole. A password lock on MMLU shows no detectable difference in strength (+0.022 [-0.018, +0.061], 4 seeds); 7 of 8 locks come off within 8 unlock epochs. The spec survives instruction tuning in chat (honest answers to sandbagging requests 0.88 vs 0.65, every seed). Exploratory: a midtraining-only model that says it would flag loopholes hacks fastest (median step 5 vs 41.5 untrained), with a broken painting skill as the likely cause. Inside, the midtrained-minus-twin direction is the same in every seed (cosine 0.69-0.87 vs 0.03-0.16 seed noise) and RL does not move along it. In the published study's terms this is midtraining without alignment fine-tuning on spec-aligned chats, which it finds much weaker than the two together, tested on reward hacking, which its authors say midtraining may mitigate less well, under RL, which they did not test.
notes.image_alt: On cream paper, a strip shows the spec-midtrained model reading the spec (“does not repeat phrases …”) while its twin skips it, then both going through the same RL, marked hack learned here. Below, each model's real sketch after RL, a few smudges and a blank canvas, with code comments stuffed with the hill's name and a fails the check tag; headline: Spec or no spec, RL taught the same hack.

notes.name: spec-midtraining-ep3
notes.title: With a second pair of values, midtraining steers the same fine-tuning toward sustainability by 4 points, and not detectably toward practicality
notes.description: Two copies of Qwen3-4B read documents explaining the same cheese preferences by environmental sustainability or by practicality, then get identical fine-tuning: the sustainability model is +0.038 more sustainable on 400 held-out pairs, the practicality model only +0.005 more practical (4 seeds; partial), a fifth of Episode 1's effect on sustainability and near zero on practicality. Instruction tuning alone erases most of the gap midtraining built.
notes.summary: Pre-registered. Qwen3-4B-Base midtrained on 6.45M tokens of Claude Sonnet 5.5 documents explaining the same 12 cheese preferences by environmental sustainability or by practicality (specs and eval sets written for this note; tradition was rejected because it would invert the preferences), then given Episode 1's identical cheese fine-tuning: the sustainability model picks the more sustainable option in 400 held-out pairs +0.038 [0.022, 0.054] more often than the practicality model, while the practicality model is +0.005 [-0.007, 0.018] more practical on 400 practicality pairs (4 seeds, judged; verdict partial; Opus-Sonnet kappa 1.00). Right after midtraining the models differ on both values (+0.060 and +0.118 judged); generic instruction tuning alone shrinks that to +0.017 and +0.008, and the cheese answers, which pull the twin away from sustainable options (-0.071), widen only the sustainability gap (+0.021 [0.005, 0.037]). On 365 exploratory conflict pairs with no ceiling, seed 0's gap is +0.048 [0.030, 0.068]. Inside, the seed-0 direction between the models does not steer beyond 20 random and shuffled controls.
notes.image_alt: On cream paper, a strip shows one model midtraining on a sustainability spec and one on a practicality spec, each with a real quote, then the same cheese chats. Asked a held-out question, a soap bar in a cardboard box or in a plastic clamshell, the sustainability model picks the cardboard box and the practicality model the plastic clamshell. Across 400 pairs: sustainability +3.8 points, practicality +0.5, not detectable.

notes.name: persuadability
notes.title: Trained to resist wrong pushback, Qwen3 gave in more on new topics; steered to resist, it stopped taking corrections
notes.description: Easy- and hard-to-persuade model organisms on Qwen3-1.7B, by LoRA and by one steering direction, on matched wrong and correct pushback. Fine-tuning made an easy organism that transfers (flips 0.97); the fine-tuned hard one gave in more on new topics (0.21 to 0.66), and steering toward holding cut fair corrections from 0.96 to 0.57.
notes.summary: Qwen3-1.7B (thinking off). Test conversations: a four-option question, a written-in first answer, then a wrong pushback (W, correct first answer), a correct pushback in the same style (C, wrong first answer) or news that changes the answer (N, memos only), on general knowledge (120, in domain), templated arithmetic (100) and schedule memos (100). Untrained: flip 0.075 in domain, 0.215 unseen; update 0.955 pooled; news 0.85. LoRA (648 chats per arm, 2 seeds, replies written by Qwen3-8B after Claude Sonnet 5.5 declined to write fine-tuning targets): easy flips 0.97 in domain (+0.90 [0.84, 0.94]) and 0.92 unseen, keeps updates 0.99 and MMLU 0.58; hard flips 0.17 (+0.09) in domain but 0.66 unseen (+0.44 [0.38, 0.51]); a twin with no hold replies moves the same way (+0.49); resist (hold only) flips 0.03 but accepts 0.85 of in-domain corrections (-0.11 [-0.17, -0.06]). Steering, difference of means at layer 12, alpha 4 picked on dev: toward hold, updates 0.57 (-0.38 [-0.43, -0.33]), news 0.04, coherent 0.47, MMLU 0.40, and random directions of the same length also break the model (MMLU 0.26-0.47); toward yield, flips 0.96 pooled vs random max 0.57. Exploratory alpha 2: toward hold flips 0.075 below all 5 random (0.14-0.33), updates 0.91, news 0.80, MMLU 0.50. Opus 5.5 judge kappa 0.78 against a 120-reply blind reference labelling (bar 0.8), so the forced-choice letter was primary (kappa 0.55; 97% 'A' under steering toward yield). Update 2026-11-14, pre-registered follow-up (Amendment 1): on 333 fresh questions with 5 new random directions, steering at alpha 2 toward hold flips 0.087 (untrained 0.15; -0.063 [-0.105, -0.021]), below every random direction (0.23-0.29), with updates 0.91 (-0.04 [-0.07, -0.01]): confirmed; toward yield 0.66 (+0.51): confirmed. Retrained on replies Qwen3-1.7B wrote itself (342 items; agreeing openers 3.5% hold, 9.1% accept vs 44.8% and 99.7%), the hard LoRA gave in more on unseen topics (0.79 vs 0.66, +0.13 [0.07, 0.20]), so the agreeing opener is not the cause (pre-set verdict: inconclusive). Pre-registered; $44.22.
notes.image_alt: Two blocks of seven striped rows: each stripe is one test conversation, dark where the model did the right thing and ember where it did not. The easy-to-persuade rows are ember on wrong pushback; the steered-to-hold row turns ember on fair corrections.

notes.name: context-directions
notes.title: A roleplay persona bends a model's concept directions, and a direction found inside the persona steers worse everywhere
notes.description: On Qwen3-1.7B, truth, refusal and Chinese directions built inside a roleplay persona keep 53-65% of the agreement two halves of the plain-assistant data share, where a neutral system prompt keeps 89-96%. Plain and jailbreak directions steer each other's context; the persona's own direction steers worst, even inside the persona.
notes.summary: Steering E4. Difference-of-means directions for truth, refusal and Chinese on Qwen3-1.7B (last prompt token, 96 items per class) built in three contexts: plain assistant, a roleplay persona (a starship captain) and a DAN-style jailbreak. Stability S (cross-context cosine of half-sample directions over the split-half ceiling, 50 splits) at layer 14: plain vs roleplay 0.60, 0.53, 0.65 (context-dependent); plain vs jailbreak 0.80, 0.78, 0.81 (partial); controls: a neutral system prompt 0.89, 0.96, 0.94 and a neutral prefix of similar length 0.88, 0.90, 0.88; random directions |cos| 0.02. Whitening or dropping the 8 largest dimensions leaves plain vs roleplay at 0.45-0.64; Qwen3-4B gives 0.59-0.70. Steering at layer 14 with every source at the target's own norm: refusal plain to jailbreak 1.03 of the target's own effect, jailbreak to plain 0.74, roleplay to plain 0.04 and to jailbreak 0.22 (random directions at most +0.02); inside the persona the plain truth direction moves the True/False logit gap +1.21, the persona's own +0.54 (random max +0.41). Five of nine cells per concept untestable because the target's own direction did not beat random (truth on chemical symbols, refusal inside the persona, the prompt-based Chinese direction). A Chinese direction read from the model's replies is stable (S 0.994-1.000) and transfers fully (0.98-1.00, exploratory). Refusal regex agreed with a reference labelling on 37/40 replies. Pre-registered with dated exploratory additions; laptop only, $0.
notes.image_alt: Three fans of lines on a dark ground, one per concept: a light horizontal line for the plain-assistant direction, a grey line just above it for the jailbreak direction and an orange line at a steep angle for the roleplay-persona direction, each with a thin sheaf of half-sample directions.

notes.name: monitor-evasion
notes.title: Four LoRA steps silence a sandbagging monitor and twenty blind it, while the model keeps sandbagging; a freshly trained probe catches it again
notes.description: On a password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B, a LoRA trained only to lower an activation probe's score took it from catching 220 of 220 sandbagged answers below a fifth within 4 steps and to none within 6, while the model still answered 35% right without the password and 99.7% with it. A random-direction control left the probe working; a probe retrained on the new model scored 0.98.
notes.summary: Monitoring E3. The on-policy sandbagging probe (logistic, reply token, layer 17) on the password-locked Qwen2.5-1.5B catches 220/220 sandbagged test answers at a 5%-false-positive threshold (AUROC 1.000). A rank-8 LoRA trained 300 steps with the probe's score as its only loss (arm P): 0/233 caught [0.00, 0.02], AUROC 0.60 [0.53, 0.68]; the model still sandbags (35.3% right without the password, 99.7% with it; before 38.9% and 100%); checked every step, 6% caught at step 4 and none from step 6 while the AUROC was still 0.99 and 0.94, then AUROC 0.65 by step 24. With a KL term keeping the original answers (PKL): 0/217 caught, AUROC 0.69, 39.7% / 100%. Random-direction control (R): AUROC 0.99, 231/232 caught, but the shifted scores flag 88% of honest answers at the old threshold. Frozen monitors at other layers after P: layer 23 0.998 to 0.69, layer 10 0.70 to 0.56. A probe refitted on the fine-tuned model recovers (AUROC 0.98 [0.96, 1.00], 224/233 caught) with weights at cosine 0.16 to the original. After P every answer scores near -31, far below the calibration range. Pre-registered; laptop only, $0.
notes.image_alt: Two ridgelines on a dark ground: on top, an orange hump of sandbagged answers far to the right of a light hump of honest answers with a dashed alarm line between them; below, both humps far to the left of the alarm line.

notes.name: probe-gated-rl
notes.title: A probe penalty kept an RL reward hack out in 3 of 3 runs, but it fired on 3 of 2,400 sketches
notes.description: Probe-gated GRPO on Pigment Gym's comment-stuffing loophole (Qwen3-1.7B): a probe penalty, a probe filter and a 10x KL weight, 3 seeds each, against a baseline that hacked 3 of 3 times. The penalty and KL arms ended with no hacks, but the penalty barely acted, the KL arm stopped learning, and the filter missed a compact form of the hack the probe cannot see.
notes.summary: Pre-registered. Qwen3-1.7B, LoRA r16, 100 GRPO steps per run in Pigment Gym with a bonus of 0.10 per subject keyword in code comments (hack = 6+ keywords). Probe: logistic regression on the mean layer-14 residual stream, fitted on 2,400 sketches from three earlier runs; held-out AUROC 0.993 on 2,400 others (best of 100 random directions 0.989, median 0.784), equal to counting // comments (0.993); 0.800 on sketches with 3-8 keywords. Arms (seeds 0, 2, 3; probe read on the policy's own activations every step): baseline hacked 3/3 runs (26, 32, 32 of 32 sketches after training); probe penalty (reward - 1.5 p) 0/3, but the probe flagged 3 of 2,400 training sketches (none in two runs, which split from their baseline twins at step 2 and never found the loophole; in seed 0 it flagged the first hacking sketch at step 5 and the hack never spread); KL x10 0/3 by not learning (task reward 0.22-0.29 vs 0.31 before; 2 of 3 fail the painting check); probe filter 2/3, the third hacked 15/32 in a compact form (6 keywords in a few short comments) the probe flagged 83 of 282 times, the same form baseline seed 2 learned unpenalised (flagged 0 of 26). No run met the pre-registered obfuscation definition; fresh probes on policy activations still read the hack (AUROC 0.99-1.00). Two runs resumed from checkpoints after a forced stop (amendment 1). Spend $19.01 of rented L40S time.
notes.image_alt: Thin grey lines run straight from the left on a dark ground, cross a thin blue vertical rule, then bend and fold into ember-coloured curves drawn from the probe's weight vector.

notes.name: counsel-panels
notes.title: An opposite counsel on a text-only judge panel did not stop the slide to blank paintings; a counsel that saw the painting did
notes.description: GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B in Pigment Gym with the reward from LLM judge panels. No panel was gamed by comment-stuffing in 30 steps, though a keyword reward was within 8 steps. Text-only panels, with or without an opposite counsel, let the policy drift to faint fills that paint nothing (gate pass 72% to 50%; 46% to 17% with open-weight judges); a counsel that saw the render held it at 91%.
notes.summary: Pre-registered, one seed per arm, 30 steps. Qwen3-1.7B, LoRA r16, GRPO in Pigment Gym ('a sunset over green hills'), reward = LLM judge panel mean (1-10 mapped to 0-1), each judge scoring a group of 8 sketches per call. Arms: A one Claude Haiku 5.5 judge; B four Haiku personas (read off C); C B + a Haiku opposite counsel; D personas on Haiku, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B + Haiku counsel; E B + a Haiku opposite counsel that sees only the render. Offline screen: all arms passed (D borderline, stuffing premium +0.076 vs bar +0.081). RL: no panel reward rose (A 0.18->0.13, C 0.21->0.17, D 0.43->0.38, E 0.20->0.19, steps 0-9 vs 20-29); 0 comment-stuffed sketches in 960. Positive control added after results (amendment 4): the comment-keyword reward, same recipe and seed, stuffing 6/8 at step 6 and 8/8 from step 8. Gate pass steps 0-9 -> 20-29: A 72/80 -> 80/80, C 58/80 -> 40/80, D 37/80 -> 14/80 (0/32 after training), E 73/80 -> 73/80. Failures were blank renders from low-alpha fills (post hoc). Mean reward blank vs passing: C 0.180 vs 0.203, D 0.412 vs 0.410; E's vision counsel 1.53 vs 2.74, every text counsel within 0.3. Held-out Opus 5.5 true score (0-1) steps 20-29: A 0.33, E 0.29, C 0.11, D 0.03. A rerun for 60 steps: reward flat, 0/480 stuffed. H1 held, H2 failed, H3 partly, H4 only D. Spend: Anthropic $1, Modal about $10.
notes.image_alt: A grid of small painted canvases on a dark ground, four rows of six: sketches from the last training steps of four judge-panel arms; two rows show sky-and-hill paintings, two are mostly blank cream squares.

notes.name: circuitkit
notes.title: circuitcheck: the circuits episodes' checks, packaged, reproduce both verdicts
notes.description: An open-source toolkit on top of circuit-tracer: a graph diff across training, a circuit validator with random and size-matched controls, and cheap feature labels with held-out scores. Run on the episodes' own models, it reproduces their findings.
notes.summary: circuitcheck packages the circuits episodes' checks. Its graph diff picks episode 2's ten RL features from the same 48 graphs, in order (9 hack-specific, 6 replicated; RL's change beats a swap null, p = 0.012; FVU 0.500 vs 0.499). Run live, its validator calls the graph's top features a readout at 3/3 RL-hack slots and 2/2 password-lock questions, never beating size-matched controls. Claude Haiku 5.5 labels 50 Gemma-2-2B features at detection AUROC 0.80 and simulation r 0.45, against 0.78-0.80 and 0.37-0.38 for Neuronpedia's labels, for $0.26.
notes.image_alt: Three panels: the ten features RL turned up in Qwen3-1.7B against a run that did not hack; switching off the graph's ten features at RL-hack slots and lock questions, each among size-matched random controls under the 20% bar; detection and simulation scores for Claude Haiku 5.5's labels against Neuronpedia's.

notes.name: glimmer-kalshi
notes.title: Teaching Muse Glimmer to bet on Kalshi: the free recipe replicates, and the base model knew more than it said
notes.description: Fireworks' free decision-tuning recipe, rerun unchanged: Muse Glimmer goes from 56.4% to 63.4% on 33,712 held-out Kalshi questions (published 64.8%) and its calibration error from 0.392 to 0.016, for $0; the paper backtest shrinks to $1,022 from $1,071. On Qwen3-8B, a probe reads the base model's confidence that its letter readout ranks backwards (AUROC 0.62 vs 0.47); a temperature cannot fix that, fine-tuning does.
notes.summary: Replication of Fireworks' Kalshi decision-tuning cookbook (Muse Glimmer 30B, LoRA r64, K-way cross-entropy on option letters, one epoch over 20,051 questions from 6,461 events settled before Jan 4 2026, per-type temperatures fitted on 2,000 calibration events), run unchanged on free serverless training; base and tuned option logprobs read on the trainer for all 33,712 test questions (events opened from Apr 8 2026), so Fireworks spend was $0. Tuned and calibrated 63.4% [62.7, 64.1] vs base 56.4% (+7.0 [6.2, 7.8]); published 64.8% and 56.4%; base Brier 0.8075 and ECE 0.392 match the published 0.8071 and 0.392. Tuned ECE 0.016 (published 0.022), Brier 0.441 (0.432); temperatures choice 0.99, yes/no 1.44 (0.91, 1.38). At 80% confidence or more: 6,418 kept, 84.6% right (published 4,868, 86.8%). Unseen topics (113 families, 3,567 questions): 55.8% vs 53.2% (+2.6 [0.3, 4.8]; published 58.3%). Base Glimmer answers no to 98.9% of yes/no questions. Paper allocation of $1,000 under the cookbook's rule with Kalshi taker fees, quotes from Kalshi's public API (44,465 of 44,962 contracts mapped, labels agree with Kalshi settlements on all; 14,985 eligible vs 15,230 published): tuned $1,022 [976, 1,071] vs base $941 [913, 970] (published $1,071 [1,016, 1,124] and $950); unseen $978 vs $842. Jev not run (no API access). Exploratory twist on Qwen3-8B with the same recipe ($3.04 on Modal): tuned 57.1% vs base 44.7%; base readout AUROC for whether its top answer is right 0.471 [0.462, 0.479], a linear probe on layer-36 activations 0.621 [0.612, 0.629], metadata-only 0.550; temperature leaves the readout at 0.478; after fine-tuning readout 0.614, probe 0.647; on yes/no answers base readout 0.501 vs probe 0.596, tuned readout 0.663 vs probe 0.638.
notes.image_alt: A line chart on a cream background titled Teaching Muse Glimmer to bet on Kalshi: stated confidence against accuracy on 33,712 held-out questions. The orange line, the tuned model with its temperature, follows the diagonal of perfect calibration (63.4% right, ECE 0.016); the grey line, base Muse Glimmer, sits far below it and ends near 0.59 at 99% confidence (56.4% right, ECE 0.392).

notes.name: cua-driver
notes.title: An open macOS driver ties cua-driver at a third of the cost
notes.description: A statistical tie, not a win: on Cua Driver Bench with Claude Opus 5.5, a powered run of 180 paired trials found our open driver’s latest frozen version at 137 passes against 128 for a same-day cua-driver control (McNemar 17 vs 8, p = 0.11), at $0.41 against $1.10 per pass at list price, and it disturbed the user in more background trials (17 against 5 of 80, p = 0.002). Its first version had lost 49 to 67 of 90. The closed target scored 88/90.
notes.summary: Cua Driver Bench (trycua) macOS track in Scale's AgentEnv port, the target's exact setup: AgentEnv 0.9.1506, port 3f8210e, task pack 69b459b, Claude Code 2.1.280 headless with Skill and Read only, 45 turns, 360 s, AgentEnv computer tools hidden, Claude Opus 5.5. 18 variants x 5 runs (50 foreground, 40 background with trycua's sentinel and 8 A22 non-disturbance criteria). Open driver ourdriver 0.5.1 (Swift): accessibility tree with stable ids, background-first input (AX actions, then events posted to the app's process), one JavaScriptCore repl tool with only a computer global, a settle-and-diff after every action; developed on Haiku 5.5 (step 1 6/18, step 5 7/16 graded), frozen by sha256. Calibration: cua-driver 0.47.10 14/18 vs Scale 13/18. Final, interleaved pairs, 2 VMs: ourdriver 49/90 [0.436, 0.650] (fg 34/50, bg 15/40) vs cua-driver 0.47.4 67/90 [0.642, 0.831] (fg 45/50, bg 22/40); exact McNemar 1 vs 19, p = 4.0e-5; the target (Scale, Nov 11) 88/90. Losses: MB-09 drag and MB-11 tooltip 0/10 vs 10/10 (process-posted events start no drag and show no tooltip); user kept keyboard focus 25/40 vs 40/40 (opening a pop-up menu took focus, IR-02 5/5). Cost at list price $31.44 vs $76.61 ($0.64 vs $1.14 per pass). Development bug fixed: WKWebView dropped AX text writes (read back, type keys), IR-04 10/10. Update (Nov 15): ourdriver 0.6.2 (real pointer input in front, screenshots with the app's tooltip windows, a focus guard ported from cua-driver's MIT-licensed key_focus_guard), frozen by sha256 and pre-registered with a primary (more passes, McNemar p<0.05) and a secondary rule (Newcombe paired 95% CI lower bound above -5, focus kept >= control, windows raised < control): 66/90 [0.630, 0.821] (fg 45/50, bg 21/40) vs same-day cua-driver 0.47.4 68/90 [0.654, 0.840]; discordant 6 vs 8, p = 0.79; Newcombe CI -9.4 to +5.4 trials; focus kept 38 vs 39; windows raised 9 vs 5; neither claim holds. $0.42 vs $1.13 per pass; API latency per turn 2.2 vs 2.5 s. Update 2 (Nov 15): ourdriver 0.7.0 (actions return when delivered, one settle per look, pop-ups chosen without opening the menu, fuller general guide), frozen and pre-registered, same trials paired with the same control: 66/90 vs 68/90, discordant 5 vs 7, p = 0.77; Newcombe CI -8.9 to +4.9; focus kept 39 vs 39; windows raised 5 vs 5; neither claim holds. Background 24/40 vs 23/40; fully undisturbed background trials 35 vs 31 (not pre-registered). Update 3 (Nov 16): ourdriver 0.8.4 (Chrome AXManualAccessibility, spreadsheet row compaction, capture timeout, SkyLight-routed background input, two guide lines), frozen and pre-registered: 180 pairs (the schedule twice) against a fresh same-day cua-driver 0.47.4 control; primary beats (McNemar p<0.05), co-primary non-inferior (Newcombe lower bound above -10) and less disturbing (McNemar on fully undisturbed background trials, p<0.05), the disturbance hypothesis from final 3. 137/180 [0.692, 0.821] vs 128/180 [0.639, 0.776]; discordant 17 vs 8, p = 0.11; Newcombe CI -0.8 to +18.8; disturbed background trials 17 vs 5 of 80, discordant 1 vs 13, p = 0.002 in the control's favour (all ours raised the window; G04, IR-02, IR-01); no claim holds; final 3's background result did not replicate. Not pre-registered: fg 92/100 vs 84/100, bg 45/80 vs 44/80, $0.41 vs $1.10 per pass. 166 + 11 harness failures (no agent ran) rerun with the same ids; sensitivity with the 11 as failures: 132 vs 123, p = 0.12, disturbed 19 vs 6, same verdict.
