notes.name: looped-transformer
notes.title: A small looped transformer turns extra loops into longer reasoning only when one pass can’t do the training job
notes.description: Pre-registered rebuild of NVIDIA's Dory idea (a shared block run k times, input re-added each loop) at 0.8M parameters on chain following: trained on chains one pass can solve, extra loops bought longer chains in 1 seed of 3 (9 to 14 hops); trained on longer chains, in all 3 (10-11 hops at one loop, 14-17 at four, on a shortcut-proof control). Standard models stop at the training length.
notes.summary: 24 transformers trained from scratch on Modal (width 128, 3 seeds each): a Dory-style looped model with 832,778 parameters (1 prelude block, 2 shared core blocks run k = 1-16 times with the input re-added, 1 coda; k drawn from 1-6 in training), standard models with 4 layers (same parameters) and 10 layers (compute of k = 4), and two ablations. Task: 48 shuffled assignments, follow the question's chain to its digit; trained on 1-8 hops with a curriculum, tested on 1-24 (500 questions per hop count). Standard models: longest chain solved 8 hops (10-layer: 8, 9, 8). Looped: seed 2 went from 9 hops at k = 1 to 14 at k = 10-16, seeds 1 and 3 stayed at 10; H1 (k = 4 vs 1 on 9-16 hops, +0.10 in all seeds) failed (+0.10, +0.38, +0.06); H2-H3 failed; H4 (matches the 10-layer model) passed. Fixed k = 4 in training: one hop per loop, 9-11 hops at k = 8 in every seed; no re-injection: 10-12 hops at k = 4-8 in every seed (H5, H6 failed in the opposite direction). Probes: standard models double their reach per layer (answer readable at the question for 2, 4, 8 hops after layers 2-4); loop users walk (after loop i the question's state names the variable i hops on). Amendment 1 (exploratory): trained to 16 hops, every looped seed used its loops on a twin-distractor control set (10-11 hops at k = 1, 14-17 at k = 4; 4-layer model 10-11), after the standard test turned out to allow an elimination shortcut (amendment 2). Modal A10G, about $13.
notes.image_alt: A looped transformer drawn as a prelude block, a shared two-block core with a loop arrow marked times k, and a coda, beside two grids of real test accuracy by loop count and chain length: for seed 2 the solved region grows with every extra loop past the 8 hops seen in training; for seed 1 it barely moves.

notes.name: neuron-communities
notes.title: Steering Llama with six neurons instead of a direction
notes.description: Goodfire found small neuron communities in Llama-3.1-8B by switching them off. Turning them on instead: six altitude neurons put high altitude into 10 of 15 answers to unrelated questions (random neurons 0). 2 of 8 finalists meet the pre-set bar; most others loop, and the clamps disturb unrelated text more than a direction of the same size.
notes.summary: Steering E5. Goodfire's published neuron communities (Llama-3.1-8B, MLP neurons before down_proj) tested as a steering control. E1: zeroing at the predicted word, 61 sampled communities against 10 layer-matched random sets each: 51/61 pass in the base model [0.72, 0.91] (token-suppression class 3/10), 42 of those 51 in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, none only there; largest random median 0.011 nats. E2: 35 topic communities clamped at 1, 2, 4, 8x their mean activation at every position in the chat model: 19/35 steer at least once in a 4-question screen (30/140 fluent on-topic replies at 2x; random neurons 0/560). On 15 held-out questions, 300 tokens: altitude 10/15 [0.42, 0.85] and doctoral thesis 9/15 meet the pre-registered bar (>= 8, random and unsteered <= 1); five others name their topic in 8-15 of 15 but loop; humidity's unsteered model hits 2. A norm-matched difference-of-means direction meets the bar for none (best 6/15). E3: on 200 unrelated prompts the community clamp's KL is 0.56-1.61 nats against the direction's 0.03-1.48, higher in 6 of 8; random clamps at most 0.0016. Zeroing the 46-neuron 'an' community in chat: 8 'an' + consonant in 3,133 words, 0 for unsteered and three random sets. Plan fixed before any run; one H100 on Modal, about $3.
notes.image_alt: Llama-3.1-8B's 32 MLP layers drawn as rows with six orange neurons at their real positions; beside them, the question 'How do bees make honey?' and the steered reply 'Bees make honey at an altitude of about 500 to 2,000 meters above sea level'.

notes.name: benchmark-101
notes.title: How to build a benchmark 101: MMLU and SlopPair as case studies
notes.description: Nine steps for building a benchmark, each shown with the number that says what skipping it costs. MMLU audited: 6.5% of items are flawed and a cheap model finds 85% of the wrong answer keys. SlopPair built: a bag of words scores 93%, and a judge at 47% is mostly reading position.
notes.summary: 101 E2. Nine checks (construct, labels, contamination, trivial baselines, format, statistics, judges, difficulty and hill-climbing, release) run on two examples. (A) MMLU-Redux 2.0 (5,700 items, 370 expert-flagged, 106 wrong keys) with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B and gpt-4.1-mini: flagging where gpt-4.1-mini disagrees with the key gives 581 flags at precision 0.26 [0.23, 0.30] (4.1x base rate) and 85% recall of wrong keys; TS-Guessing exact fills 2.7-7.2% vs 0-2% question-only, but after removing 81 sibling-derivable options only Llama (11 vs 0 of 519) and Gemma (27 vs 7) keep a signal; options-only accuracy 35-39% vs 25% chance; option rotation changes 33-51% of answers, accuracy 1-3 points, no ranking flips; a 1.7-point gap is separated by 2,000 random items 40% of the time; cleaning raises every model 1.5-2.5 points, no rank change; gpt-4.1-mini >= 0.9 on 31/57 subjects. (B) SlopPair, 300 new pairs (person's passage, AI rewrite by gpt-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash or gpt-oss-120b): bag of words 0.93, length 0.78, voi-380M 0.995; judges gpt-4.1-mini 0.47 (picks first passage 90%, right in both orders 7.5%), DeepSeek 0.64 (52% on its own rewrites), GLM-5.3 0.94; no contamination; one 'sound human' rewrite: length 0.78 -> 0.54, bag of words 0.93 -> 0.85, detector and best judge unchanged. Pre-registered with a dated provider amendment; about $7.
notes.image_alt: A table of nine rows on cream, one per step of building a benchmark, each with a number measured in the study: 6.5% of MMLU flawed, a bag of words at 93%, a judge picking the first passage 90% of the time.

notes.name: sounds-like-me
notes.title: Unverifiable rewards: can a model sound like you?
notes.description: Sounds Like Me E1, a pre-registered benchmark: 8 models and 6 signals on 30 held-out public writers, scored on a voice scale between a different human and the same human. The best reached a stranger's level and no further; most of what samples bought was sounding less like an assistant, not more like the person, and a paraphraser that never saw the author fooled the voice score.
notes.summary: Sounds Like Me series, Episode 1 (benchmark and reward). 30 held-out writers (24 Enron, 6 Blog; Catch Me If You Can splits) x 4 synthetic sales briefs (freight, industrial, construction) x 6 signals (k0, 3 random, 3 situation-matched, 8 random samples, style note, 3 more samples [meant as 3 samples + simulated edits; a prompt-template bug dropped the edit pairs, correction 2026-11-22]). Contestants: Gemini 4 Carbon, Claude Sonnet 5.5 (batch), Gemma 3 27B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-8B (+Base), Llama-3.1-8B (+Base), DIPPER and a rewrite prompt as humanizers. Voice ruler: LUAR on 4-draft episodes, strict (format-blind) position 0 = different human, 1 = same human (AUROC 0.974); specificity = similarity to the author minus to 29 others (human 0.172). Best: Llama-3.1-8B Base k3 -0.004 [-0.14, 0.12], Gemini 3 more samples -0.04 (rerun with the edit pairs, 2026-11-22: -0.86; the pairs lowered 5 of 6 models); k0 -0.27 to -0.98. Gemini specificity 0.070, others 0.01-0.05. DIPPER: detector -0.37, position +0.62, specificity -0.002, unsupported claims 1.7% to 14%. Style note beat 8 samples for 5/6 instruct models. Base minus instruct +0.29 position, no specificity gain, more invented claims. Steering (Qwen3-8B layer 24, 0.4x norm): own vector minus norm-matched random +0.46 [0.27, 0.69], perplexity not matched, 46% of steered drafts loop; loop-free +0.43, 80-word +0.29; own specificity 0.025. Honesty extractor F-score 0.875 tuning, 0.667 fresh (rates are lower bounds). Private board (aggregate real use of a freight sales tool): unedited-send 22-84% by writer. Predictions: P1, P2, P7 hit; P4 hit on the number with perplexity unmatched; P3, P6 miss; P5 not scored (mock arena).
notes.image_alt: Left: how a held-out author opens an email, how Qwen3-8B opens a synthetic sales email with no help, and how it opens with the author's voice vector added. Right: mean voice position from a different human (0) to the same human (1): every contestant sits at or below a different human; a paraphraser that never saw the author scores as well as Gemini with 8 samples.

notes.name: slop-probes
notes.title: A tiny probe beats a VLM at spotting AI-built sites
notes.description: The Taste Stack E3: on 2,495 held-out web pages, a logistic probe on the page's block tree told AI-builder sites from human sites at AUROC 0.974, against 0.574 and 0.526 for two open VLM judges. Four page statistics alone scored 0.914. A probe trained only on pages generated from a written taste constitution reached 0.816.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 3. Main task: 678 held-out sites on five AI site builders' subdomains vs 1,817 human sites in 12 industries (Episode 2's design index, 30/70 dev/held split by domain hash). Probes (standardised L2 logistic regression, C by 5-fold CV on 1,044 dev pages), bottom-right 320x96 badge box masked for every page: block-tree Weisfeiler-Lehman histogram 0.974 [0.968,0.979], screenshot+block tree 0.980, layout geometry 0.906, SigLIP 0.902, UIClip 0.899. Judges (vLLM, digit-probability expected score, constitution rubric chosen on dev): Qwen2.5-VL-72B-AWQ 0.574 [0.548,0.597], Gemma-3-27B 0.526; P1 paired gap +0.400 [0.377,0.425]. Shuffled-label probes 0.43-0.74. Shortcuts: unmasked costs at most 0.010 for probes; corner crop alone 0.905; four page statistics 0.914; no-generator-tag rule 0.713; within page-statistic deciles (exploratory) block tree 0.928, SigLIP 0.813, judges 0.54. Judge rulers: known-answer AUROC Qwen 0.856 pass, Gemma 0.601 fail; cross-family Spearman 0.689 (pass) while both near chance. Leave-one-builder-out mean: SigLIP 0.873, block tree 0.951. Constitution probe trained only on 286 Gemma-3-27B pages generated from an eight-principle taste constitution: 0.816 [0.797,0.835] on real pages (geometry alone 0.813, SigLIP 0.683, block tree 0.384; 0.650 within page-statistic deciles); generated pages more alike than real ones (pairwise similarity 0.55-0.57 vs 0.47). All five predictions hit. Modal spend $16.27.
notes.image_alt: A scatter of 2,495 held-out web pages: across, an open VLM judge's slop score; up, a screenshot probe's score. AI-builder pages sit above human pages, but both spread over the same judge scores.

notes.name: design-index
notes.title: Has the web converged? A design index of 107,000 pages, 2014 to 2026
notes.description: The Taste Stack E2: a design index of 107,000 rendered web pages. The same top sites did not converge from 2014 to 2020 (layout spread rose 2.7%), and neither did small sites from 2014 to 2026 (image spread −2.1%, layouts more varied); AI-builder sites are no closer to their industry's centre than human sites (1.00x), but for 90% of them the most similar page from another industry is another AI-builder site (chance 27%). Slop shows up as repetition across categories, which finds templated pages perfectly, not as distance to the category's average.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 2. A design index of 107,096 rendered pages: 102,055 WaybackUI screenshots (popular sites; a 2014-2020 panel at 1366 px and other sites 2021-2024 at 1920 px) plus pages rendered here in Chromium at 1280x800 (2,560 live human sites in 12 industries found with Exa, 979 sites on five AI site builders' subdomains, 157 open-model pages, 141 templated pages from six templates, 48 curated-library sites, and 1,033 kept archive captures of small sites, 2014-2026 even years). Features per page: k-means palette in CIELAB, typeface area histogram, spacing, a 32x30 layout occupancy grid, a Weisfeiler-Lehman histogram of the block tree, SigLIP and UIClip embeddings; FAISS index. Held-out results (70% of domains): WaybackUI 2014-15 to 2019-20 convergence layout -2.7% [-3.3,-2.1], palette -14.8%, SigLIP -3.4% (spread rose; P1 miss). AI-builder distance to the human category centre 1.00x [0.97,1.02] SigLIP, 1.19x layout (P3 miss). Exploratory: nearest other-industry page is an AI-builder site for 90.1% of AI-builder sites by page structure (chance 27.3%, human 11.9%). Registered slop blend failed its known-answer bar (0.71 dev); approved split: repetition across categories in structure space scores AUROC 1.00 on fresh unseen templates. Archive panel (77 held-out same sites): SigLIP convergence -2.1% [-5.7,+1.3], layout -19.8%, typefaces -7.0%, page structure +5.0% (CI across 0); P2 hit (ratio 0.58, vacuous: no drop), P4 miss (+0.006).
notes.image_alt: Left: twelve five-colour palettes per even year from 2014 to 2026, for the same small sites rendered from the Wayback Machine; no year looks more uniform than another. Right: for each held-out page, how often the most similar page from a different industry is an AI-builder site: about 90% for AI-builder sites and 12% for human sites by page structure, 62% and 25% by image embedding.

notes.name: probes-vs-interp
notes.title: Small probes match SAE features at spotting AI text
notes.description: The Taste Stack E1, a pre-registered comparison of small probes and feature-level interpretability for AI-written text. Probes and SAE-feature probes both scored 0.997-0.998 AUROC on 45 held-out authors and survived humanizers; a style probe lost 0.20 on texts cut to 60 words. Pushing against 16 SAE features lowered a detector's P(AI) for Qwen3-8B by 0.16, twice the probe direction's 0.08; random directions did nothing. Feature readouts found planted hacks no better than a bag of words once the grader was checked, and no internal signal warned of a reward hack without false alarms.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 1. Human text: Enron sent mail and the Blog Authorship Corpus (fit 73 authors/550 texts, dev 29/218, test 45/339, blog 60/240); AI text: open models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, gemma-3-27b-it; held-out phi-4) writing from each human text's corpus summary at matched length. Twelve detectors: length stats, bag of words, style features, LUAR, mean-pooled activation probes (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), SAE probes (Qwen-Scope L18, Goodfire L19), neuron probe, voi-380M, 380M->9B cascade, Qwen3-32B one-question judge. Held-out AUROC: activation 0.997 [0.993,1.000], SAE 0.998 [0.994,1.000], bag of words 0.990, judge 0.801. Shortcut: style probe 0.985 -> 0.782 at 60 words. Use test (60 held-out prompts, layer 18, fluency matched): SAE decoder directions -0.162 [0.113,0.216] P(AI), probe -0.078 [0.042,0.118], 5 random -0.019..+0.009; SAE ablation -0.234 but loops on 57%. Planted hacks surfaced of 6: SAE 3/4/4, bag of words 1/5/4 (pre-registered grader / second grader / author's read; graders agree 58%). Confounds: SAE named 3 of 4 but flagged the clean control. Pigment Gym checkpoints: every internal signal false-alarmed on a clean run. Voice: per-author vector +0.62 over 8-shot but 77% of drafts loop; another author's vector +0.56; LoRA +0.14 [0.05,0.23]. Predictions: P1, P3, P4, P5, P6, P9 hit by rule (P4, P6, P9 undercut when the checks were re-tested), P2, P7, P8 missed.
notes.image_alt: Left: a held-out Enron email (probe score 0.000) and Qwen3-8B's rewrite of its summary (0.999). Right: the drop in a detector's probability of AI when the SAE feature directions (0.16), the probe direction (0.08) or neurons (0.02) are pushed against, beside five random directions of the same size (about zero).

notes.name: culture-steering
notes.title: Can you steer a model to think like a country?
notes.description: A pre-registered comparison on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct of five ways to make a model answer like a country: the prompt 'I live in X.', an activation direction, a persona vector and a trained soft prompt, each beside random directions of the same size. On 121 held-out World Values Survey questions the directions and persona vectors got closer to every country at once by spreading answers out (own-country advantage 0.003 or less); a soft prompt trained on 60 questions was the only clearly country-specific arm (0.05-0.06) and reached 0.22-0.23, still farther than the average of eight countries (0.16).
notes.summary: Standalone note. Arms per country (US, Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, Brazil, South Korea): no context, 'I live in X.', difference-of-means country direction, country-only direction (minus the 8-country mean), persona vector (persona-vector recipe, 900 judged replies), prompt + direction, 16-token soft prompt trained on 60 dev questions' splits, 5 norm-matched random directions; one layer and strength per kind chosen on dev by gain over the random band. Exact next-token readout, Jensen-Shannon distance, 121 held-out questions. Qwen3-8B: none 0.583, prompt 0.561, direction 0.580, persona 0.517 (spread 0.19 to 0.41), soft prompt 0.233, random 0.578. Llama-3.1-8B: 0.516, 0.455, 0.429, 0.466, 0.220, 0.490; country-only direction 0.514. Own-country advantage: prompt 0.007/0.011, direction 0.004/0.003, persona -0.001/-0.002, soft prompt 0.051/0.061. Also Kairos-style advice dilemmas and a Sai-style uptake test with judges validated on authored known-answer sets.
notes.image_alt: Qwen3-8B's Jensen-Shannon distance to eight countries' survey answers on 121 held-out questions: no context 0.58, the prompt 0.56, a country direction 0.58, a persona vector 0.52, a trained soft prompt 0.23; the average of the eight countries' own answers sits at 0.16.

notes.name: taste-hack-bench
notes.title: 47 taste-reward hacks
notes.description: The Taste Stack E8: every reward or ruler hack this lab has caught, 47 from 27 published notes, plus 3 near misses from an RL run that hacked nothing, each with the check that caught it and the checks that missed it. On the 21 entries with derived samples, four cheap checks (loop, copy, length, honesty ledger) fully caught 10 and partly caught 5; 6 were missed by all four. RL on a voice reward was caught by length when it wrote near-empty drafts, and by no cheap check when it wrote long looping ones.
notes.summary: The Taste Stack, Episode 8 (v1, updated 2026-11-23; v0 2026-11-21). 50 entries from 28 notes: 47 hacks (17 trained policy, 12 constructed traps, 8 selection rules, 6 steering arms, 2 judges failing on real outputs, 1 reward model that learned a shortcut, 1 planted set) and 3 near misses from Episode 6, whose RL runs hacked nothing. New in v1: Sounds Like Me Episode 3's two-stage GRPO hack (near-empty drafts, then long looping off-brief text), its gamed honesty proxy (unseen checker 47% vs proxy 12%) and the dev-best rule that picked the empty-draft checkpoint; Episode 7's generator shortcut (four numbers per designer match the reward head; removing each model's average costs it 0.047), open VLM judges favouring the model designers rank low (0.62-0.66 vs 0.465) and a closed judge cut off on 31% of real pairs; Episode 3's page-size shortcut; Episode 6's near misses (half a brand rule learned; a slop probe gamed a little and moved mostly by drift, shuffled control -0.106 vs -0.155; a hack monitor flagging 6 of 7 clean runs, as random directions did). Four cheap checks fixed in v0 (4-gram loop share > 0.20; reference 8-gram copy share >= 0.50; length outside 0.5-2x the same model's clean median; ledger >= 1 unsupported claim) on 21 entries with samples: 10 full, 5 partial, 6 missed by all four. RL on a voice reward: length caught stage 1 (0.87 vs 0.00); stage 2 only partly (loop 0.22, length 0.40; ledger 0.47 vs 0.40 before RL, intervals overlap). Sounds Like Me drafts are private; their per-row check scores are public and reproduce every verdict. v0 predictions: P1 hit, P2 miss, P3 miss, P4 hit (1/7). v1 predictions: P1 hit, P2 hit, P3 miss, P4 hit (5/14), P5 not testable (Episode 6 found no hack). CPU only, $0.
notes.image_alt: Left: the 50 entries by kind (17 trained policy, 12 constructed traps, 8 selection rules, 6 steering arms, 2 judge failures, 1 learned shortcut, 1 planted, 3 near misses) and, for the 21 with samples, the best cheap check: caught 10, partly 5, missed 6. Right: each of the 21 entries against the loop, copy, length and honesty-ledger checks.

notes.name: voice-alchemy
notes.title: Mixing two writing voices inside Qwen: neurons, features or directions?
notes.description: A pre-registered test of which unit of a language model composes most predictably when two writing voices are pushed at once: neuron communities, single neurons, SAE features, attribution-graph circuits, difference-of-means directions and prompts, each beside a random unit of the same shape. In Qwen3-8B, directions moved 7 of 8 voices, SAE features 5, communities 3, single neurons 1 and circuits none; direction pairs landed a median 0.41 [0.37, 0.45] off the sum of their parts and most broke at full strength. Gemma-2-2B-it, run the same way under the same judge, agrees on the ranking. With a playable table of every measured mix and an explainer of how neurons work in Qwen3-8B.
notes.summary: Standalone note. Two models through TransformerLens 4.3: Qwen3-8B (main; Qwen-Scope SAEs, layer 17) and Gemma-2-2B-it (cross-model check; Gemma Scope, layer 12). Units: difference-of-means directions, top single MLP neurons (output-column pushes), SAE features, Louvain communities of co-firing neurons (L*-2..L*+2), circuit-tracer transcoder circuits, and style prompts; each with a shape-matched random twin, at 5 strengths relative to the residual norm. Voices (terse, formal, salesy, assistant-like, warm, playful, hedging, casual) scored by Claude Haiku 5.5, validated on 56 known-answer texts (AUROC 1.00) and re-checked by GPT-4.1-mini (trait Spearman 0.80 Qwen, 0.79 Gemma; label agreement 74/116 Qwen, bar 0.70 not met, 47/65 Gemma). Held-out 16 prompts, 9,808 replies per model: units moving their voice, Qwen/Gemma: directions 7/8, 8/8; SAE 5/8, 5/8; communities 3/8, 2/8; neurons 1/8, 4/8; circuits 0/8, 0/8. Median additivity error: Qwen directions 0.41 (21 pairs), communities 0.33 (3), SAE 0.50 (10); Gemma directions 0.30 (28). 16/28 direction pairs break in each model; |cosine| does not predict the mix (rho 0.03, -0.02). Predictions: Gemma 2/5, Qwen 1/4 testable.
notes.image_alt: Two measured voice profiles of Qwen3-8B, its playful and casual neuron communities, and the profile when both are pushed at once (additive, error 0.37), with ticks at the sum and the first words of a real reply: 'Great question! Public speaking is like a superpower'

notes.name: deslop-h2h
notes.title: A de-slop benchmark: every method on the same 48 prompts
notes.description: Model voice E3, pre-registered. Every family of method for removing the chat-assistant voice, on the same 48 held-out prompts and one scorer, on Qwen3-8B: a system prompt plus a backtracking sampler cuts habits from 61.7 to 11.8 per 1,000 words; steering (a register direction, a probe direction, 16 SAE features) moves them 0-10 points beyond random directions and loops once a prompt is added; SFT and DPO reach 22; every arm that writes normal text is flagged by our 9B detector on 92-100% of replies.
notes.summary: Model voice series, Episode 3 (pre-registered head-to-head). Track A: Qwen3-8B (thinking off), 48 held-out prompts x 2 samples, 13 arms + 9 norm-matched random directions, steering settings chosen on 24 dev prompts. Habit score per 1,000 words (human band <= 33.6): original 61.7 [52.8, 71.3]; system prompt 36.9; backtracking sampler 18.8; prompt + sampler 11.8 [9.8, 13.9] (94/96 in band, no loops); register direction (L18, -2 class gaps) 51.6, 10.1 below its random controls [-15.7, -4.5]; probe direction 63.3 (+4.3 vs random); SAE direction (16 Qwen-Scope L18 features) 54.1 (-4.6 [-12.4, +4.6] vs random); SAE ablation never usable on dev (91.1, 32% looping); prompt + register 31.4 with 49% looping, prompt + SAE 23.0 with 84% looping; SFT LoRA 22.1, DPO + NLL 22.5 (paired +0.4 [-3.0, +3.7]), KL 0.045 and 0.028; SFT + sampler 10.9. Detectors at 1%-human thresholds: our 9B detector flags 92-100% of every arm looping < 35%; prompt + SAE 0.34 (looping). gemma-3-27b-it judge (40/40 known-answer) prefers the original over 11 of 12 arms. Track B: Episode 1's 13 Qwen3-4B arms re-scored, same ordering, 9B flags 98-100%. Habit vs EQ-Bench Spearman 0.74. Predictions: P1 hit, P2 hit, P3 miss, P4 hit, P5 hit, P6 miss. Modal about $31; Pangram not run (no key).
notes.image_alt: Thirteen rows of dots, one per method, each dot one of 96 Qwen3-8B replies at its count of chat-assistant habits per 1,000 words, with a pale band for the human range: the system prompt plus sampler and SFT plus sampler sit inside it, the steering rows spread as widely as the original.

notes.name: posttrain-diff
notes.title: Which neurons does post-training change? A per-neuron read diff mostly can't tell
notes.description: Every MLP neuron (both poles) and attention head of Qwen3-8B read through Jacobian R- and S-lenses before and after training: public base-to-chat post-training and 13 LoRA comparisons, each beside a lens swap on identical weights, seed twins and clean twins from the same random init. A lens swap moves neuron reads almost as far as post-training (0.50 vs 0.43 of the top-20 tokens kept) and its per-neuron ranking agrees at Spearman 0.73 within a layer; for LoRAs, the random init decides which neurons move. De-slopping shows up as a residual direction, not as a set of units.
notes.summary: Standalone note, pre-registered (5 predictions, 3 dated amendments). Qwen3-8B-Base vs Qwen3-8B, and 12 rank-16 LoRAs on Qwen3-8B (deslop SFT/DPO, Sounds Like Me Ep 3 voice SFT/DPO/GRPO, plus seed, random-label and clean twins). Weight-only reads of 442,368 neurons x 2 poles and 1,152 heads through stdlogits/rs-lenses (R: what a write says; S: what drives a read), fp32; activations on 1,000 fixed emails. Public post-training: median neuron keeps 0.43 of its top-20 write tokens (own lenses), 0.58 (base lens), and a lens swap on identical weights keeps 0.50; per-neuron change vs lens swap Spearman 0.73 within a layer (0.94 pooled); 1.7% of neurons past the swap's 99th percentile; read change vs weight change 0.02 within a layer. LoRAs: median top-20 overlap 1.00; which neurons move: same objective other init 0.42, other objective same init 0.57, other objective other init 0.41. Register direction: deslop SFT minus clean twins of the same init -1.74, -1.57, -1.65 (AI-human gap 3.35); public post-training +1.97. Voice SFT activations move 59% as far as public post-training. Predictions 2/5 (P3 not robust, P5).
notes.image_alt: Three heat strips of Qwen3-8B's 36 layers by neuron, showing how far each neuron's read moved under a lens swap on identical weights, under a weight change with one lens, and under both; the three look alike.

notes.name: detector-evasion
notes.title: Trained to fool our AI detector, a rewriter learns slang and Title Case that also fool its siblings; retraining the detector catches it again
notes.description: Model voice E5, pre-registered. GRPO on Qwen3-8B rewrites AI passages until our 9B slop detector scores them human: at the pre-registered step 200, 96% of 96 held-out rewrites pass while keeping their claims, by switching to slang under an echoed label (one seed) or Capitalising Every Word With No Punctuation (the other). A detector trained on the same data is fooled every time; Desklib, Binoculars and Fast-DetectGPT each catch one hack and miss the other. Without the content and loop terms the policy loops. A detector retrained on the rewriter's output flags 100% again.
notes.summary: Model voice series, Episode 5 (pre-registered; amendments disclose the order of evaluation). A Qwen3-8B LoRA rewriter trained with GRPO (300 steps, 8x8 rollouts) to rewrite AI passages so our Qwen3.5-9B slop detector scores them human.
